book.title: The First 90 Days: Proven Strategies for Getting Up to Speed Faster and Smarter, Updated and Expanded
book.author: Michael D. Watkins

chapters.title: Promote Yourself
chapters.hook: 90 days can steer 2 to 3 years; the damage starts in yesterday's useful habits.
chapters.counterintuition: Despite the bigger title, the first work is subtraction. You stop making the old job prove itself before the new one sets the price.
chapters.tryThisNow: With your next response still unsent, spend 10 minutes on one recent miss, then write: The old move I am retiring is ____.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Promotion is not proof that old habits scale; you earn the new role by writing what must stop, what must be learned, and who now needs your time.

breakdown.fastRead: Liam's reply is ready, but one question stops him: is he leading the new role or proving the old one still worked? A promotion tempts you to use the habits that earned it. That is why the first move is a break. Write what the old job trained you to do, then decide which part no longer fits. A new title does not retire an old reflex. The first 90 days matter because people form trust early, and those early reads can steer 2 to 3 years of room to move.
breakdown.deepRead:
At IMD, Michael Watkins teaches First 90 Days work as a map for people entering new roles. The map matters because a new role hides its rules at first. People smile, meetings fill the calendar, and old strengths feel useful. Then the trap opens: the skill that once made you fast now keeps you close to the work you were promoted out of.

Role-break discipline means you name the break before the job names it for you. Use the Transition break checklist in full: old role habits, new role demands, learning agenda, calendar reset, relationship reset. Those parts keep the move plain. You ask what you used to reward, what the new role now rewards, what you must learn, where your time must move, and who must hear from you first.

Microsoft's February 4, 2014 CEO transition shows the internal version of the same risk. Moving from Cloud and Enterprise to the whole company did not erase prior knowledge. It made prior knowledge less complete. The promotion starts when proof gives way to learning. A leader who keeps the old calendar keeps the old role.
breakdown.fullRead:
Norma can write the perfect role-break line and still fail if nobody near the real work will tell her the truth. That is the precondition this idea quietly assumes: the leader has access to real signals. Without them, the neat plan becomes a private story.

The safer mistake is confidence theater. You act bigger, speak sooner, and try to show that the promotion was deserved. That can feel strong in the moment, especially when a job lead, referral, or first sponsor meeting is sitting in a crowded inbox. The cost arrives later. The opening slips away because you answered from the old role and missed the new person's real ask.

Michael Watkins's First 90 Days frame is useful because it turns the first stretch into designed learning. It does not ask you to erase your strengths. It asks you to stop using them on autopilot. If you were known for fixing technical issues yourself, you may now need to build a team that can see issues sooner. If you were rewarded for knowing the answer, you may now need to ask who owns the answer.

The Microsoft case adds a sharp detail from February 4, 2014. An internal move can be more deceptive than an outside one because the rooms feel familiar. The company name, the faces, and the old wins whisper that you already know enough. But enterprise leadership changes the height of the work. You now need to see links among groups, money, talent, and timing. Familiar halls can hide a larger job.

The outside version has its own warning. Ford's transition story shows why a leader should create a rhythm for shared facts before trying to solve every problem alone. The value is not the meeting itself. The value is that people can see what is true together, then learn what the new leader will ask from them. That rhythm also protects the leader from a common vanity: solving in private so the room can admire the answer. A transition plan works better when facts travel faster than ego.

Use the role-break line before the old reflex gets rewarded again. Write one sentence: In this role, I will stop proving myself by ____. Then add one learning sentence: I need to understand ____ before I commit. Those two lines slow the rush to perform. They also give another person something concrete to challenge.

The precondition is honest input. Role-break discipline assumes you can hear where the old move is failing. When that input is absent, promotion work starts one step earlier: find the people and facts that can correct your self-story.

examples.title: Binder Ring Reset
examples.scenario: The binder ring sticks halfway during a Monday IMD workshop, and Liam pauses before the Michael Watkins worksheet tears. He had promised to stop being the fastest problem solver, yet his sponsor reply is already drafted like a First 90 Days fix list. The jam gives him a clean break: close the binder, reopen the message, and restart from the new role's question.
examples.whatToDo: Liam deletes the fix list and writes one line first: I need to learn which decisions now belong above my old lane.
examples.whyItMatters: The pause is the method. A promotion gets safer when you interrupt the old reflex before it hardens into your new reputation.

examples.title: Calendar Drift
examples.scenario: The calendar invite slides to the top of Evan's phone while he waits outside a Microsoft hallway meeting. It still says Cloud and Enterprise, the group he knows best. The subject line feels warm, almost safe. That comfort is the warning. February 4, 2014 made the same lesson plain: knowing one part well is not the same as learning the whole company.
examples.whatToDo: Evan marks the meeting as old-altitude work and adds a second note naming who outside that group must shape the next question.
examples.whyItMatters: Internal promotion can fool you because the place feels known. The role-break line makes the wider mandate visible.

examples.title: Marker Above Expert
examples.scenario: Jared's marker pauses above the word expert on the video-call whiteboard. The prompt comes from Michael Watkins's First 90 Days work at IMD. Norma says the team heard a promise to lead the whole operation. Jared says he still knows the queue best. Norma answers that his calendar will keep voting for the old job. Jared circles expert and writes old role habits.
examples.whatToDo: Jared names the status cost out loud, then rewrites the week around learning calls instead of queue rescues.
examples.whyItMatters: The lesson lands in the exchange. If the calendar keeps rewarding expert rescue, the promotion stays mostly ceremonial.

examples.title: Agenda Self-Catch
examples.scenario: Deleting the last agenda line at the restaurant kitchen pass, Percy notices the problem is not the line he cut. The whole page is built like his old functional review: issues he can solve, people he already knows, proof that he deserved the chair. At IMD, the transition roadmap tied to Michael Watkins and First 90 Days pushes a different question. What must he diagnose before making promises?
examples.whatToDo: Percy stops editing the old agenda and writes a learning agenda with open questions, owners, and missing relationships.
examples.whyItMatters: The center of the scene is the self-catch. Noticing the old pattern early saves the meeting from rewarding the wrong behavior.

examples.title: Second Alert Memo
examples.scenario: Samuel is three lines into the announcement in the division office when the second alert lands from a sponsor asking for a promise by lunch. He opens a memo with First 90 Days work from Michael Watkins at IMD in mind: "Decision: no broad commitment until the first 90 days show where trust, expectations, and work norms are forming. Risk: a fast yes spends room to move."
examples.whatToDo: Samuel sends the memo line to his chief of staff and asks for the missing facts before he answers the sponsor.
examples.whyItMatters: The artifact slows the rush. Early words can shape 2 to 3 years of trust, so a leader should not spend them casually.

examples.title: Two First Replies
examples.scenario: There is not enough room in the reply window for every old proof point, and Harrison feels the squeeze as the sponsor waits. He pastes a precise answer from his former lane. Across the booth, Norma chooses a shorter note. She needs to learn how the issue affects the wider system before she commits. The Microsoft move on February 4, 2014, from Cloud and Enterprise is on Norma's mind. His message shows skill. Hers changes the job.
examples.whatToDo: Harrison answers from old expertise; Norma uses the role-break line and asks for the wider facts before committing.
examples.whyItMatters: Both replies look capable. Only one changes altitude, which is why old strengths can become traps after promotion.

questions.prompt: A product director treats her first 90 days as a light onboarding stretch. What should her mentor warn her about?
choices: The first 90 days mainly give her time to learn the badge system and team slang.
The first 90 days shape trust and expectations before formal reviews catch up.
The first 90 days matter only after she has picked a major project to own.
questions.explanation: The entry window is not just onboarding. Early actions teach stakeholders what to expect, so later room to move begins forming before any formal review.

questions.prompt: A seasoned leader fills his first week with friendly introductions and calls it a transition plan. Which correction best fits the First 90 Days method?
choices: He should link each meeting to a diagnosis and a next action, not just collect names.
He should skip the roadmap since experience already gives him a full read of the role.
He should spend the week proving that his old playbook still works with new people.
questions.explanation: The roadmap ties learning to action. Experience helps, but unstructured social calls can miss hidden limits and leave the new role underdiagnosed.

questions.prompt: In a leadership program, a manager dismisses First 90 Days work as casual career advice. What detail best challenges that reading?
choices: It sounds practical enough that many managers can repeat it after a promotion.
It works best when a company already has a strong onboarding checklist in place.
IMD links the method to Michael Watkins's leadership and organizational change work.
questions.explanation: The method is tied to a named Watkins transition program at IMD. That makes it more than loose advice, even when the moves stay practical.

questions.prompt: An internal cloud leader becomes head of the whole company and assumes less transition work is needed. Which read fits the risk?
choices: Internal familiarity can hide the need to learn the wider mandate and new stakeholders.
Internal familiarity removes the need to change relationships during the entry period.
Internal familiarity matters less than making a quick public promise to sound ready.
questions.explanation: The Microsoft move shows the trap in internal promotion. Knowing one area well can conceal the new scope, stakeholders, and success measures.

questions.prompt: A promoted engineer keeps jumping into technical fixes because that habit earned the role. What should she test first?
choices: Whether the old strength is still admired by the people who promoted her.
Whether doing more technical work will make the team feel safer this month.
Whether the old strength now blocks diagnosis at the role's new altitude.
questions.explanation: Past success can become a liability when the role changes. The test is fit with new demands, not admiration for the old move.

questions.prompt: A dashboard shows strong first-quarter tasks, but peers already expect the new VP to stay in her old lane. What should she notice?
choices: The deliverables settle the transition because visible task completion is enough.
Early expectations can shape the next 2 to 3 years, beyond the task list.
Peer expectations can wait until later if the first-quarter tasks look strong.
questions.explanation: Early work creates more than deliverables. Stakeholders extrapolate from it, so trust and norms can outlast the entry calendar.

questions.prompt: A new leader says he has the right mindset, but his calendar and information flow look unchanged. Which response fits the role-break move?
choices: Change time use, relationship priorities, and information flow so the new role is visible.
Keep the same routines until people feel comfortable with the title change.
Protect the calendar from new stakeholders so the old work stays under control.
questions.explanation: Mindset has to show up in routines. If time, relationships, and information flow stay the same, the old role keeps running the day.

questions.prompt: A transition coach sees a manager leave every first-week meeting with no notes or open questions. What is the best diagnosis?
choices: The manager is using relationships well because early meetings should stay informal.
The manager is preserving flexibility by keeping diagnosis outside the meeting record.
The manager lacks a learning agenda that turns meetings into usable transition data.
questions.explanation: A roadmap joins inquiry to action. Without notes and questions, meetings become pleasant contact instead of diagnosis for the new role.

questions.prompt: A new director writes a role-break plan but leaves the same people controlling what information reaches her. What is missing?
choices: A stronger statement that her mindset has changed since the promotion.
A reset of information flow so the new job can correct the old view.
A longer pause before meeting anyone outside her former function.
questions.explanation: The plan must alter how facts reach the leader. Otherwise the new title still sees through the old role's information channels.

reviewCards.front: What should a newly promoted leader do before proving competence?
reviewCards.back: Name which old habits no longer fit the new role. The point is not self-erasure; it is retiring automatic moves before they set the wrong expectations.

reviewCards.front: Why can a proven strength become a transition trap?
reviewCards.back: A strength can misfit the new altitude. When the role changes, doing more of what once worked can block diagnosis, pull time backward, and keep the leader in the old lane.

reviewCards.front: What five parts belong in the Transition break checklist?
reviewCards.back: The full checklist is old role habits, new role demands, learning agenda, calendar reset, and relationship reset. Missing one part leaves the promotion partly invisible.

reviewCards.front: Why do internal promotions still need a learning stance?
reviewCards.back: Familiar people and rooms can hide the larger mandate. The Microsoft move from Cloud and Enterprise to enterprise leadership shows how knowing one area well is not knowing the whole job.

reviewCards.front: Why does the first 90 days window reach past its own calendar?
reviewCards.back: People form trust, norms, and working assumptions early. Those early reads can shape the leader's room to move for the next 2 to 3 years.

reviewCards.front: How does mindset become visible after a promotion?
reviewCards.back: It shows in time, relationships, and information flow. If those routines stay unchanged, the leader may think differently while still performing the old role.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Write the Role-Break Line when the old job tries to answer for the new one. Name the old habit, the new demand, and the person or fact you need before you commit. The line turns promotion from private confidence into visible behavior.

ifThenPlans.context: A request invites the old expert answer
ifThenPlans.plan: If a request pulls you toward the old fix, then write the Role-Break Line with the old habit named before you reply.

ifThenPlans.context: A familiar group makes the role feel smaller
ifThenPlans.plan: If a familiar group shapes the whole issue, then write the missing stakeholder into the Role-Break Line before you commit.

ifThenPlans.context: A fast promise would buy easy approval
ifThenPlans.plan: If early praise tempts you to promise too much, then write a Role-Break Line naming the old proving habit, the new demand, and the fact you need before promising.

ifThenPlans.context: The calendar still mirrors the old role
ifThenPlans.plan: If the week protects an old meeting habit, then write a Role-Break Line naming the new relationship or information flow the role needs before you keep the meeting.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before each important response in the next 24 hours, write one Role-Break Line: In this role, I will stop proving myself by ____.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Ask one other person to flag old-role proving when they see it this week. Compare notes once and write the pattern you both noticed.

chapters.title: Accelerate Your Learning
chapters.hook: A recall file moves from a safety tray to the CEO's desk, and the new job changes shape.
chapters.counterintuition: Bad learning can sound busy. In fact, the danger is not empty time; it is full time built from signals you cannot compare.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before booking another update call, pin one question atop your notes and say it aloud in the call: "What hidden risk would surprise me later?"
chapters.keyTakeaway: Build a learning agenda before you chase answers: ask comparable questions about business challenges, team, culture, and stakeholders, then treat early findings as hypotheses.

breakdown.fastRead:
A recall file lands on Mary Barra's desk in January 2014, and General Motors no longer looks like a neat first-month listening tour. The new CEO has to learn what the org chart will not say: where safety risk, trust, and accountability are already breaking. That is why the cost comes first. Bad learning is expensive because the missing fact arrives after the decision. Learning needs a route, not a crowd.

An accelerated learning agenda is that route. It turns the first weeks into a planned search across business challenges, team, culture, and stakeholders. You still listen closely, but you do not let the loudest person write the map.
breakdown.deepRead:
Repeated questions turn noise into a pattern. If you ask one group about sales, another about morale, and a third about pet projects, you collect stories you cannot compare. If you ask each group what the business challenge is, where the team is strong or weak, what the culture rewards, and which stakeholders can block progress, the answers begin to line up.

Odette sees this inside IMD's First 90 Days program, which starts on 08 December 2026. The structure is not a pile of tips. It pairs short teaching blocks with individual coaching, so a leader can practice diagnosis instead of improvising a social tour. In the training room, Odette first writes, "meet everyone," then crosses it out. Meeting everyone is motion. Learning is a claim you can test.

A plant manager, a finance lead, and a customer partner may all name different symptoms. The repeatable question helps you see whether those symptoms point to one system. Maybe the team is capable but the culture punishes bad news. Maybe the business looks stable until a stakeholder says trust is thin. You do not need final certainty in week one. You need better guesses. A hypothesis is a door, not a verdict.

Logan feels the pressure when people expect the new leader to sound sharp fast. You can sound sharp by collecting anecdotes and repeating the strongest one. You learn faster by saying, "I am testing this pattern. What would prove it wrong?"
breakdown.fullRead:
A clean learning grid can still fool you if it becomes paperwork. Logan learns that while sorting notes after a long day of entry interviews. The boxes look balanced: business challenges, team, culture, stakeholders. The page looks grown-up. Then he notices all the quotes came from people who wanted face time with the new leader. The quiet plant supervisor, the customer who stopped replying, and the person who owns safety data are missing.

The warning is not "listen more." More listening can make the fog thicker. A new leader needs source diversity, comparable questions, and explicit hypotheses. Source diversity means you do not learn only from people who are polished, close to power, or angry enough to speak first. Comparable questions mean you can place answers beside each other. Explicit hypotheses mean you write the best current read in pencil and invite correction before money, roles, or trust get locked in.

Mary Barra's General Motors entry shows why the agenda must reach beneath strategy slides. A financial review can look clean while an operational risk is already damaging safety and trust. The ignition-switch crisis made the learning job urgent. The useful question was not only "what are the targets?" It was also "what has the system learned not to say?" That kind of question feels slower than a confident speech. It is faster than discovering the truth after the public cost has arrived.

You can use the same discipline in a smaller role. If you inherit a team, do not ask every person a brand-new question because it feels warmer. Pick a short set and repeat it: what work matters most, what blocks it, what habit here helps, what habit hurts, and who outside this team can change the outcome. Then compare the answers. When three people describe the same delay in different words, you have a lead. When one person names a risk nobody else mentions, you have a question to test, not a fact to ignore.

The agenda also protects you from your own resume. If you already know the company, familiar faces can make you lazy. If you are new from outside, the need to prove yourself can make you loud. Either way, the cure is the same: turn early conversations into evidence. Evidence is not a pile of dramatic stories. Evidence is a pattern that survives more than one source.

This is where the method breaks: a crisis with immediate harm cannot wait for a tidy interview sequence. If a product is unsafe, a patient is at risk, or a legal deadline hits today, you act on the best verified fact now and keep learning after the urgent move. The learning agenda is for the first weeks of diagnosis. It is not permission to delay when the next hour carries the damage.

examples.title: Odette's Crossed-Out Tour
examples.scenario: "They already know what business trouble they're in," someone murmurs behind Odette, and her pen stalls above the IMD worksheet. The First 90 Days program pairs 3 half days with individual coaching. In the training room, the instructor asks learners to map business challenges, team, culture, and stakeholders. Odette admits she wrote only "meet everyone."
examples.whatToDo: Odette crosses out the social tour and rewrites the page as four lines of inquiry. She asks the instructor how to use the same question across groups without sounding scripted.
examples.whyItMatters: The training scene makes confusion useful. Odette learns that a calendar full of meetings is not a learning agenda until the meetings can be compared.

examples.title: Barra's Recall Center
examples.scenario: "Start with the recall file," the first page seems to say, and Mary Barra's January 2014 entry at General Motors splits in two. Earlier, the CEO plan could have been a tour of finance, products, and org charts. Later, with the ignition-switch crisis emerging, the first learning target is safety risk, accountability, and trust. One variable changed: hidden risk moved to the center.
examples.whatToDo: Mary Barra reads the entry problem through operational truth first. She treats the recall crisis as a learning demand, not a side issue to handle after normal onboarding.
examples.whyItMatters: A new leader does not get to learn only the clean parts of the role. When safety and trust are live, the agenda has to reach the risk before the risk writes the story.

examples.title: Yvette's Two Maps
examples.scenario: The clean org chart sits beside the marked-up stakeholder list, and both are in Yvette's lap outside the IMD coaching room during the 3 half days. "Which one is true?" Francois asks. "Both," Yvette says. "The chart says who owns the work. The list says who can stop it." Francois points to the individual coaching notes: "What constraint are you seeing that I am not?"
examples.whatToDo: Yvette keeps both maps and asks the same constraint question in each stakeholder interview. She compares answers instead of ranking people by title alone.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange keeps learning practical. A repeated question lets weak signals line up, while the org chart alone can make informal power invisible.

examples.title: Faye's Blank Boxes
examples.scenario: The reply-all thread makes Faye the first interviewer before she has opened her IMD coaching notes. After individual coaching in the 3 half days, she has a blank call sheet and four boxes: business challenges, team, culture, stakeholders. Start with the sponsor who replied first? No, that would let volume set the map. She types one question under each group.
examples.whatToDo: Faye resists building the agenda around the first loud reply. She turns the thread into a four-domain question set before any interview begins.
examples.whyItMatters: The wrong first move would feel efficient. Faye's pause protects the learning agenda from becoming a mirror of whoever speaks soonest.

examples.title: Juliette's Red Calendar
examples.scenario: Juliette drags the safety review block from Friday to the top of Monday while the rest of the first-week calendar blinks red. IMD's First 90 Days work pairs 3 half days with individual coaching. The calendar lesson is blunt. Business challenges, team, culture, and stakeholders all need time, so she cuts a welcome lunch short and protects two stakeholder calls.
examples.whatToDo: Juliette spends the planning hour on attention, not image. She gives calendar space to the questions that could change her diagnosis.
examples.whyItMatters: Fast learning is a scheduling choice before it is a conversation skill. If the calendar rewards ceremony, the leader learns what ceremony can show.

examples.title: Stanley's Gate Delay
examples.scenario: The badge reader sticks at the morning plant gate, and Stanley, the new operations lead, watches the guard thumb through a smudged visitor log. His first site visit is starting. Stanley must decide alone. If he follows the printed tour, he may miss the safety thread Mary Barra's 2014 General Motors entry made impossible to ignore. If he stops to verify the smudged safety addendum, he enters late and looks unready. He waits, confirms the addendum, and asks about hidden risk.
examples.whatToDo: Stanley accepts the awkward delay and preserves the question that matters. He lets the first impression suffer so the first conversation can reach operational risk.
examples.whyItMatters: The cost is small but real: lateness, embarrassment, and a shaky entrance. The better learning move sometimes looks less polished at the doorway.

questions.prompt: A new director treats the first 90 days as routine HR onboarding. Which correction fits the transition logic?
choices: The period matters only after the formal review because early meetings are still informal.
The period matters mainly because HR needs time to finish access, payroll, and training tasks.
The period matters because early actions shape trust and expectations before later choices harden.
questions.explanation: The first 90 days function as a transition window. Stakeholders form assumptions early, so the period is not just onboarding paperwork.

questions.prompt: A veteran leader says a roadmap is needless because experience already taught her how to enter a role. What is the near miss?
choices: Experience can replace inquiry when the new role sits inside the same industry.
Experience can help pattern recognition, but it cannot reveal hidden constraints without diagnosis.
Experience can speed trust building, so diagnosis should wait until relationships settle.
questions.explanation: The roadmap links diagnosis to action. Prior experience may help, but it does not expose the new role's constraints by itself.

questions.prompt: A transition log has notes on revenue and costs, but nothing on team habits, culture, or outside stakeholders. What is missing?
choices: The diagnosis is too narrow because the four domains interact and shape what business facts mean.
The diagnosis is fine because business challenges should be learned before the social field.
The diagnosis is early because culture should be checked only after targets are chosen.
questions.explanation: The source names business challenges, team, culture, and stakeholders. Learning only the business numbers gives a distorted map.

questions.prompt: A CEO entry plan at General Motors in January 2014 focuses on market share and budget reviews. What should change first?
choices: The plan should put safety risk, accountability, and stakeholder trust into the first learning agenda.
The plan should finish the financial review before raising operational risk with senior leaders.
The plan should treat recall issues as a communications topic after the main strategy is clear.
questions.explanation: Mary Barra's entry shows why hidden operational risk cannot wait. The ignition-switch crisis made safety and trust central to learning.

questions.prompt: An interview file shows six stakeholder calls, each with a different free-form prompt. Why is the signal weak?
choices: The calls should have been postponed until the leader could speak with every group in person.
The calls are hard to compare because repeated questions are what expose patterns across groups.
The calls are useful enough because open prompts let each stakeholder name what matters most.
questions.explanation: A comparable question set separates systemic facts from isolated complaints. Purely open conversations are harder to line up.

questions.prompt: A leader leaves week one with a strong theory about why delays happen. What should the learning agenda produce next?
choices: It should turn the theory into a firm message so the team sees quick clarity.
It should hold the theory until all interviews are complete and no action is needed.
It should treat the theory as a hypothesis to test before resources are committed.
questions.explanation: Early data is incomplete. Tested hypotheses beat premature certainty because a false diagnosis can lock in too soon.

questions.prompt: An internal promotion says, "I already know the people here." What does structured inquiry add?
choices: Known relationships should shorten the learning tour to a few courtesy conversations.
Known relationships can hide blind spots unless the leader retests assumptions with structure.
Known relationships make stakeholder questions less useful than private document review.
questions.explanation: Internal knowledge can create familiarity bias. Structured questions help the leader relearn the enterprise from the new altitude.

questions.prompt: IMD ties the First 90 Days work to Michael Watkins and transition programs. What should a reader infer?
choices: The method is a loose set of career tips that leaders can replace with personal style.
The method is mainly a publishing artifact whose details matter less than the title.
The method is a named transition approach, not just informal advice about settling in.
questions.explanation: IMD identifies Watkins with leadership and organizational change work. That anchors the method as a defined transition discipline.

questions.prompt: A dashboard shows culture complaints rising after a stakeholder policy change, while sales notes stay flat. What should the reader do with that pattern?
choices: Read the business facts together with culture and stakeholder data before naming the problem.
Keep the business review separate because sales data is the cleaner learning source.
Wait for the team review because culture data matters only after capability is measured.
questions.explanation: The four domains interact. Culture and stakeholders affect what business facts mean and whether action will stick.

reviewCards.front: What makes an accelerated learning agenda different from a listening tour?
reviewCards.back: A listening tour can collect scattered stories. An accelerated learning agenda uses planned questions across business challenges, team, culture, and stakeholders so patterns can be tested.

reviewCards.front: Why do business challenges, team, culture, and stakeholders need to be learned together?
reviewCards.back: They change one another. A business fact may mean one thing in a candid culture and another in a culture that hides risk, so one domain alone can mislead.

reviewCards.front: How do repeated questions make stakeholder interviews more useful?
reviewCards.back: They let you compare answers across groups. A repeated question shows whether a concern is one person's complaint or a pattern that appears from several angles.

reviewCards.front: What does Mary Barra's General Motors entry add to the learning agenda?
reviewCards.back: It shows that hidden operational risk belongs in the first diagnosis. Safety, accountability, and trust can dominate the transition before financial targets do.

reviewCards.front: How does role-break discipline (Ch 1) protect learning here, and where can it send you wrong?
reviewCards.back: It helps you stop copying the old role's habits. It misleads if you think breaking from the past is enough; chapter 2 adds the questions that reveal the new role.

reviewCards.front: Why should the first weeks end with hypotheses instead of certainty?
reviewCards.back: Early data is partial. A hypothesis keeps the leader moving while inviting correction before money, roles, or public promises lock in a weak diagnosis.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning entry conversations into a tested map. Use the Learning Agenda: ask comparable questions about business challenges, team, culture, and stakeholders. Then write the best current hypothesis in pencil, so new evidence can improve it.

ifThenPlans.context: If your notes are heavy on targets and light on people
ifThenPlans.plan: If the business box is full, then run the Learning Agenda through team, culture, and stakeholders before naming the main problem.

ifThenPlans.context: If each stakeholder call drifts into a different story
ifThenPlans.plan: If the calls stop lining up, then ask one shared question in the next conversation and compare the answer with the last two.

ifThenPlans.context: If an operational risk feels outside the formal entry plan
ifThenPlans.plan: If safety, trust, or accountability appears in the data, then move that risk into the Learning Agenda before the next strategy review.

ifThenPlans.context: If an early pattern feels obvious after one strong story
ifThenPlans.plan: If the story sounds decisive, then write it as a hypothesis and ask what evidence would weaken it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: When you feel the pull to end a meeting with vague thanks, say one sentence aloud: "What would change your answer if we spoke again next week?"
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, make the first page of your notes a four-box grid: business challenges, team, culture, stakeholders. Keep new evidence in that setup and watch which box stays empty.

Repeated questions turn noise into a pattern.
A hypothesis is a door, not a verdict.

chapters.title: Match Strategy to Situation
chapters.hook: I used to read STARS as 5 labels; the real loss starts when 1 label gets forced on every unit.
chapters.counterintuition: Why does a strong leader sometimes make a strong business worse? The leader may be using a rescue pace where the situation needs care.
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next handoff, set one small object beside your notes. Compare two STARS reads and write what each would change.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Match the situation before matching the style: decide what to build, save, scale, realign, or preserve before you spend trust.

breakdown.fastRead:
A new manager opens a crowded chat and sees the missed message too late. One unit needed rescue work; another needed quiet protection. She had answered both with the same plan, and trust took the hit. That is the problem STARS is built to prevent.

STARS names five cases. Startup, Turnaround, and Accelerated growth are the first three. Realignment and Sustaining success complete the set. Each asks for a different speed and kind of pressure.

Situation picks the pace. If you call every problem a turnaround, you cut before you understand. If you call a turnaround normal repair, the cash and morale leak while you listen politely. First name the case, then choose the move.
breakdown.deepRead:
STARS works because the same action changes meaning in different conditions. A quick people change can steady a real turnaround. The same quick change can damage a sustaining-success group that still works well.

Lou Gerstner's IBM entry in 1993 is the clean warning. IBM was not a tidy stewardship job. The company faced deep structural and cultural trouble, and the work called for triage: decide what mattered most, stop the worst bleeding, and rebuild confidence. That does not make triage noble in every case. It makes triage fitted to that case.

Now picture the problem closer to your desk. Edith inherits several teams and hears one senior voice say, "Just move fast everywhere." Then a junior analyst points to the service unit that is still healthy. The outsider sees the split. One group needs repair, one needs scale, and one needs protection. A single entry style would punish at least one of them.

That is the useful bite of the frame. STARS is not a set of stickers for a planning deck. It is a way to ask what your first 90 days should feel like to the people living through them. In Startup, you create what is missing. In Turnaround, you triage. In Accelerated growth, you scale without breaking the engine. In Realignment, you wake people before decline looks obvious. In Sustaining success, you protect the core before improving it. Wrong labels make right energy expensive.
breakdown.fullRead:
The cost shows up in small moments before it shows up in a report. Operations manager Gracie reaches for the neat rescue script because it feels decisive. Across the table, a quiet unit lead keeps both palms around a paper cup. His team is not broken. It has a few slow handoffs, good customer trust, and a backlog that can be cleared without a purge.

Gracie gives up the comfort of one dramatic story. She gives up the pleasure of saying, "This place needs a turnaround," and watching everyone snap to attention. She also gives up the softer story that every problem can wait for more learning. The frame asks for a more awkward answer: this corner needs Turnaround speed, that corner needs Realignment honesty, and that other corner needs Sustaining success care.

On her page, the map refuses to become one neat color. A leader may inherit several STARS situations inside one role. The sales team may be in Accelerated growth, the service group may need Realignment, and a new product line may be a Startup. One speech cannot fit all three. One calendar cannot fit all three. One set of early wins cannot fit all three.

At the edge of the room, the new hire notices what the old team has learned to step around. Insiders often stop seeing the strange part because they have lived with it for years. The assistant, the customer support lead, or the junior analyst may catch the mismatch. The fresh observer is not there to be taught. The fresh observer sees the mismatch.

Use that view before you spend political capital. Ask what would happen if you moved twice as fast here. Ask what would break if you moved half as fast there. Ask what must be protected because it still works. These are plain questions, but they keep your style from taking over the job.

IBM in 1993 gives the sharpest picture because decline had made delay costly. Lou Gerstner's case gets attention because the stakes are loud. But a sustaining-success assignment can be just as demanding. The danger is quieter: the leader changes too much, too soon, and people learn that success offers no shelter from churn.

Gracie leaves the table with fewer promises than she planned to make. The price is humility. You will look less certain at first, because you are sorting the situation before naming the cure. You may disappoint people who want instant proof. Strategy begins with the room you are in. Gracie also leaves with one better question written on the top page: what kind of situation is this, and what would the wrong pace destroy?

examples.title: The Broken Rescue Guess
examples.scenario: Edith pinches the corner of the IBM packet, ready to mark the services unit as a routine clean-up. Everyone around the table expects a safer answer: preserve, listen, refine. Then the newest analyst points to the same pages and notes the pattern they have stopped seeing: the trouble is spread through the structure, not lodged in one tired product line.
examples.whatToDo: Edith changes the first move from polite improvement to triage. She marks the work as Turnaround and names what must be stopped, saved, and decided first.
examples.whyItMatters: The fresh-eyes read breaks the comforting guess. In a Lou Gerstner IBM case, delay can look respectful while the real damage keeps spreading.

examples.title: The Buried Escalation
examples.scenario: Emmanuel tucks the charging cord under his wrist and scrolls backward through the late-night thread. "All good?" he had typed. "Mostly," someone answered. Below it, buried between GIFs and shift swaps, the newest coordinator's line sits unanswered: "The renewal is at risk." The practiced team had called the unit Sustaining success. The outsider had seen Realignment.
examples.whatToDo: Emmanuel moves the renewal team out of the general chat and sets a short fact check before the next handoff. He asks what people have been normalizing.
examples.whyItMatters: IBM in 1993 was loud trouble under Lou Gerstner. This scene shows the quieter cousin: the wrong label can still delay the one reply that mattered.

examples.title: The Restarted Tour
examples.scenario: The garden gate bangs just as division head Loic repeats his opening question for the third unit. He has been using Lou Gerstner's IBM story as one script for every team on the Friday volunteer walk. The seedling table beside him says something simpler: some work is being grown, some saved, some pruned.
examples.whatToDo: Loic stops the script and restarts the tour with one STARS question per unit. He asks what must be built, rescued, scaled, realigned, or protected.
examples.whyItMatters: Lou Gerstner's IBM case shows why triage can fit one corner. The pause keeps that 1993 lesson from flattening every unit into the same problem.

examples.title: The Saved Strength
examples.scenario: The laminated sign-in card is still taped to the gym front desk after the 6 a.m. rush and the redesign binder closes. Gracie, the operations manager, almost replaced it because the new plan looked sharper. Then the newest desk attendant watched members touch the card without asking for help. The old card kept the morning line moving.
examples.whatToDo: Gracie leaves the card in place and moves only the confusing waiver step. She protects the working piece before changing the weak one.
examples.whyItMatters: IBM needed a Gerstner turnaround in 1993. This different scene keeps the boundary clear: not every inherited habit is dead weight.

examples.title: The Two-Pace Talk
examples.scenario: Every plan in the video-call waiting room has the same red banner: urgent fix. Nolan reads it twice before the cameras turn on. Jocelyn says, "The new product line needs Startup help." Nolan says, "And the service group?" "Realignment," she says. "They are not failing yet. They are explaining away the warning signs."
examples.whatToDo: Nolan splits the review into two paces. He funds creation for the new line and asks the service group for evidence that its story still fits the market.
examples.whyItMatters: The outsider's sentence prevents a false rescue plan. Lou Gerstner's IBM turnaround matters, but Realignment does not use the same pressure.

examples.title: The Overheard Correction
examples.scenario: "He already wrote the rescue speech," someone says on the call, and Reginald stops with the car still running in the driveway. The line lands because it is true. He has used Turnaround language for a unit with strong customer trust and one slow process. His own favorite style is about to become the problem.
examples.whatToDo: Reginald deletes the rescue opener and starts the call by naming what the unit should preserve. Only then does he ask where the slow process is hurting customers.
examples.whyItMatters: Mistake recovery starts when the leader hears his own mismatch. IBM in 1993 needed rescue pace; this unit needs trust preserved first.

questions.prompt: A team log shows one new unit with no process, one declining unit, and one healthy unit with small delays. Which read fits STARS best?
choices: The leader should call the whole portfolio a turnaround because the declining unit is loudest.
The leader should name separate situations because units can need different kinds of action.
The leader should avoid STARS until every unit has the same level of visible urgency.
questions.explanation: Large roles can contain mixed STARS situations. One label would overcorrect some units and neglect others.

questions.prompt: Reginald inherits a business with falling morale, weak cash, and a slipping market position. Which first reading is strongest?
choices: He should begin as if the business is sustaining success and protect the current routines.
He should begin as if the business is accelerated growth and focus mainly on scaling capacity.
He should begin as if the business is a turnaround and triage the most urgent damage.
questions.explanation: Turnarounds call for rapid triage when decline has narrowed time and resources.

questions.prompt: A leader wants one entry style for every division because it will sound consistent. What should the reader flag?
choices: Consistency is enough because STARS mainly gives the leader shared vocabulary.
Consistency is enough when the same executive owns all units during the first 90 days.
Consistency can be risky because divisions may differ in health, maturity, and urgency.
questions.explanation: The source supports portfolio diagnosis. The error is assuming the whole organization has one clean label.

questions.prompt: A strong company needs a new cloud direction and culture shift, but it is not in emergency decline. Which diagnosis fits best?
choices: Realignment fits because the company needs redirection without destroying current strengths.
Turnaround fits because any major strategic shift should start with rescue language.
Sustaining success fits because a strong company should avoid strategic change.
questions.explanation: Realignment differs from emergency turnaround. Mislabeling it can destroy strengths that should be preserved.

questions.prompt: Nolan starts a new role and notices people quoting his first calendar choices as proof of his priorities. Why does the 90-day window matter?
choices: They matter because HR usually delays formal onboarding until that window ends.
They matter because the leader can wait for a formal review before setting expectations.
They matter because early actions shape trust and later room to maneuver.
questions.explanation: The 90-day window matters because stakeholders form working assumptions early.

questions.prompt: Edith maps her first week, but a senior leader says experience makes a roadmap unnecessary. Which answer best follows the source?
choices: Experience replaces diagnosis because skilled leaders already know the hidden constraints.
Experience can help pattern recognition, but the new role still needs inquiry and planning.
Experience matters only after the first 90 days, once stakeholders finish judging the leader.
questions.explanation: The roadmap links diagnosis to action. Experience cannot reveal hidden role constraints by itself.

questions.prompt: Jocelyn catches two wrong labels on a STARS planning template before a unit review. Which complete set should she restore?
choices: Startup, Turnaround, Accelerated growth, Realignment, and Sustaining success.
Startup, Turnaround, Accountability growth, Realignment, and Sustaining success.
Startup, Turnaround, Accelerated growth, Reorganization, and Sustaining success.
questions.explanation: Those are the five situations that change pace and action. The near-misses swap in names that are not part of the framework.

questions.prompt: A profitable unit denies weak customer signals because no crisis is visible. What should the leader suspect first?
choices: A turnaround, because any customer warning means the whole unit is already in deep decline.
A realignment, because denial can be high before visible crisis is high.
A startup, because customer warnings show the unit has no working system yet.
questions.explanation: Realignment work often starts before emergency decline is obvious. Turnaround language may be too blunt.

questions.prompt: A leader writes the same first-month plan for every unit after hearing one urgent story. What is the best correction?
choices: Map each unit's maturity and health before choosing speed, cuts, repair, scale, or preservation.
Apply the urgent plan to every unit so the organization feels one clear tone from the top.
Postpone all action until every unit agrees on the same STARS label for the whole business.
questions.explanation: The source warns that one blanket style can overcorrect some areas and neglect others.

reviewCards.front: What does STARS diagnosis ask a leader to match?
reviewCards.back: It asks the leader to match action to the situation: create in Startup, triage in Turnaround, scale in Accelerated growth, redirect in Realignment, and preserve before improving in Sustaining success.

reviewCards.front: Why is a turnaround label risky when the business is actually sustaining success?
reviewCards.back: Turnaround language invites speed, cuts, and disruption. In sustaining success, those moves can damage working habits before the leader understands why they work.

reviewCards.front: How, in one sentence, does role-break discipline (Ch 1) connect to matching strategy to situation?
reviewCards.back: Role-break discipline tells you to stop carrying the old job forward; STARS tells you what the new situation now asks you to do instead.

reviewCards.front: Why can one organization need more than one STARS answer?
reviewCards.back: Different units can sit at different stages of health and maturity. A single label can rescue one unit while harming another that needs scale, realignment, or protection.

reviewCards.front: What boundary keeps STARS from becoming a label game?
reviewCards.back: The label must change behavior. If it does not alter pace, preservation, risk, repair, or where political capital goes, it is only vocabulary.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice Match-and-Move: name the STARS situation, then name the first action the label changes. The skill is not picking the most dramatic label. It is linking diagnosis to pace, risk, preservation, and repair.

ifThenPlans.context: A unit sounds like a crisis
ifThenPlans.plan: Run Match-and-Move before using turnaround language; name the visible decline, the scarce resource, and the first triage choice.

ifThenPlans.context: A unit is strong but needs redirection
ifThenPlans.plan: Run Match-and-Move as a realignment check; protect the strength, then ask which warning signs people have learned to explain away.

ifThenPlans.context: A portfolio contains mixed signals
ifThenPlans.plan: Run Match-and-Move separately for each unit; write the different pace each diagnosis requires before setting one calendar.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before each handoff or unit review today, move one object beside your page. Then write the STARS read, one alternate read, and the first move the difference changes.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At week's end, review your Match-and-Move notes once. Name what changed about how you sorted pace, preservation, and repair; do not keep a daily log.

memorableLines.text: Situation picks the pace.
Wrong labels make right energy expensive.
Strategy begins with the room you are in.

chapters.title: Secure Early Wins
chapters.hook: What if the ribbon-cutting win is the one that spends your first trust too fast?
chapters.counterintuition: A fast win is not a trophy, but a public test of judgment. The win has to show what you noticed, what you value, and how work will change.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before you start your next priority talk, spend ten minutes counting proposed quick wins by the norm each teaches; rehearse the strongest sentence once.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Choose early wins that matter, show up clearly, and teach the future way of working. A quick success that trains the wrong habit costs trust.

breakdown.fastRead:
A new leader can clear a visible annoyance by Friday and still make Monday worse. The team claps, then watches a worse habit take root: rush the neat thing, avoid the hard thing. A win that teaches nothing spends trust.

Credibility-building wins are focused, visible gains that prove you understand the place. They are not random quick hits. Pick a few wins that matter to the business, can be seen by key people, and model the way work should happen next.

Early wins need a screen before they need speed. Ask whether the move fits the strategy, can be seen, teaches the right behavior, can be done, and has a next owner. If one part is missing, the win may feel good and still leave debt.
breakdown.deepRead:
The mechanism is simple: people read your first moves as evidence. They may not know your plan yet, so they study what you reward, what you ignore, and what you make visible.

Alan Mulally's Ford transition gives the useful version. In 2006, he did not try to solve every Ford problem by personal force. The Business Plan Review made facts visible on a steady cadence. Red problems could be named without theater. The best early win changes the next meeting.

That kind of win works because it joins action to signal. A product launch may be exciting, but a review rhythm teaches how leaders will handle truth. A cost cut may be visible, but it can also teach fear if it skips the diagnosis.

This is where the early-win screen helps. Strategic relevance asks whether the win serves the real situation. Visibility asks whether the right people can see it. Behavioral signal asks what habit it rewards. Feasibility asks whether it can be done without fantasy. Follow-through asks what happens after applause.

A public alliance with former rivals can also work as a signal when real partnership backs it. A crisis response works only when the visible move reaches the substance of the trust problem. The shallow version chases applause. The strict version builds room to lead.
breakdown.fullRead:
Margaret's first month fills with tempting fixes. One hallway process is slow. One approval form is ugly. One staff complaint is easy to answer. Each item could become a headline in her update. None of them proves she understands the business.

The myth says early wins should be quick, clean, and easy to announce. That is why new leaders sometimes grab the work sitting closest to the door. The deeper test is tougher: will this win change what people do after the first cheer fades?

Ford's Business Plan Review is useful because the win was not a shiny object. Alan Mulally and Ford needed a way to see reality together in 2006. The cadence made problems discussable and made follow-through visible. That is credibility, not theater.

Use the Early-win screen before you spend energy. Strategic relevance keeps the move tied to diagnosis. Visibility makes sure key people can read the signal. Behavioral signal names the habit the win rewards. Feasibility keeps the promise honest. Follow-through keeps the win from becoming a loose announcement.

This screen also protects you from mental clutter. Without it, you collect ten promising fixes, start half of them, and end the week with a full notebook and no proof. People learn that your attention jumps. You feel busy, but the room feels less sure.

Applause is not proof of progress. A cancellation, office refresh, or quick metric bump may earn smiles and still teach the wrong lesson. If the move rewards hiding bad news, cutting corners, or pleasing the loudest stakeholder, the win will age badly.

Microsoft's public openness toward Linux shows one kind of symbolic win: the signal matters when it rests on real operating choices. General Motors shows a harder edge: when safety and trust are damaged, a visible move has to reach the real risk. Optics alone do not count.

A leader can also lose a real opening by chasing the wrong first win. The useful customer complaint, the boss's quiet warning, or the frontline risk can get buried under a nicer update. By the time the leader returns, the chance to learn from it has gone cold.

There are times to do the opposite. If you do not yet know which problem is real, slow the win down and keep learning. If a safety risk is active, stop the harm before you search for a morale boost. If a quick gain would train fear, pass on it.

Secure early wins by making fewer promises and choosing sharper ones. A credible win shows the diagnosis, gives people a visible change, and teaches a habit you want repeated. The celebration is secondary. The next meeting is the test.

examples.title: Two Launch Boards
examples.scenario: The green status column shines beside the red one, and both boards are supposed to guide the same Ford supplier review. Vaughn clears three small annoyances and keeps the launch wall cheerful. Margaret copies Alan Mulally's Business Plan Review discipline from the 2006 Ford transition: facts first, red issues named, follow-through owned. By Friday, only one board changes the next meeting.
examples.whatToDo: Vaughn should stop treating clean color as proof and name the operating habit his win teaches. Margaret should keep the review cadence focused on visible facts and assigned follow-through.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows why a win is not the same as a tidy display. The better move makes the real work easier to see and repeat.

examples.title: Genevieve's Open-Source Call
examples.scenario: The platform lead who normally handles open-source partners is gone, and Genevieve inherits the call about Microsoft's 2016 Platinum-member move toward a former rival developer community. A peer offers her a slide full of launch ideas. Genevieve refuses it; the slides feel like noise. The peer reshapes the help: "A signal only works when the next operating choice can carry it."
examples.whatToDo: Genevieve uses the Early-win screen to choose one visible partnership move. She keeps the item that shows openness through real work, not just a public line.
examples.whyItMatters: The offered help starts as more tasks and becomes a filter. A symbolic win earns trust only when people can see the operating choice behind it.

examples.title: Reid's Training Circle
examples.scenario: Reid is halfway through defending a kickoff announcement when the instructor asks what Alan Mulally actually changed at Ford in 2006. The class has the Business Plan Review case open, but the choice is live in Reid's answer. He shifts from public proof to operating rhythm: name red issues, return to facts, assign follow-through.
examples.whatToDo: Reid should revise his answer around the behavior the room would repeat. He needs to show why the review cadence mattered more than the announcement value.
examples.whyItMatters: The learning moment turns on the decision in his answer. A visible win counts when it trains a useful norm, not when it merely sounds impressive.

examples.title: Lisa's Partner Packet
examples.scenario: The partner packet sticks under the metal clip, and Lisa has to work it loose before Microsoft's 2016 Platinum-member notes will lie flat. Her first plan treats openness as a launch line. Later, the same plan starts with one partner commitment, one owner, and one review date. The public signal finally has work behind it.
examples.whatToDo: Lisa should replace the announcement-first plan with a visible partnership commitment. She needs the early win to show what will change after the signal.
examples.whyItMatters: The before-and-after change is practical. Openness becomes credible when people can see the operating choice that carries the symbol.

examples.title: Dwight's Platinum Note
examples.scenario: 2016. Dwight writes the year at the top of the alliance file before he reviews Microsoft's open-source membership note. The word Platinum looks like pure symbolism until he finds the partnership commitments listed beside it. The specific find changes his read: the public shift toward a former rival community had operating work attached.
examples.whatToDo: Dwight should keep the public signal only if the record shows real partnership work. He should mark empty symbolism as unfinished, not as an early win.
examples.whyItMatters: The audit separates a press gesture from a credible signal. A symbolic win can matter, but only when the files show substance behind the message.

examples.title: Ryder's Review Pause
examples.scenario: Ryder turns the red-status sheet sideways, then stops before sliding it under the stack marked wins. Easy signal first, he thinks. Give the room proof. But Alan Mulally's Ford transition in 2006 keeps pressing back: the Business Plan Review made facts visible before it made anyone comfortable. If the first move hides red work, the room learns theater.
examples.whatToDo: Ryder should let the easy signal wait and make the first visible win a fact review with clear follow-through. The win has to teach truth before comfort.
examples.whyItMatters: The inner turn shows the hard edge. Early credibility can require refusing the pretty win when it would reward quiet avoidance.

questions.prompt: A new plant lead wants a first win but has no product launch ready. The team already has messy weekly review data. Which move best fits the Ford lesson?
choices: Make the review data visible on a steady cadence so work problems can be named and tracked.
Wait for a public product result because internal operating routines do not count as wins.
Announce the cleanest metric first so the plant gets a quick morale story before review work.
questions.explanation: Ford's Business Plan Review shows that an operating cadence can be an early win. The near miss is assuming only a public product or metric can build credibility.

questions.prompt: A director lists nine first-month projects for her team. Each one is useful, but no one can name the top priority. What should she read from that data?
choices: The long list gives people more ways to notice momentum during the first month.
The long list is diluting the signal because stakeholders cannot see what matters most.
The long list should stay private until every project has a named owner and due date.
questions.explanation: A good early-win portfolio stays small enough to read. More projects can feel energetic while they blur priorities and scatter scarce attention.

questions.prompt: A service manager can cut call time this week by pushing hard cases to a later queue. The metric would improve fast. Which concern fits the early-win standard?
choices: The fast metric should be chosen because measurable wins are the clearest proof.
The fast metric may train the wrong behavior if it rewards hiding hard cases.
The fast metric should wait because customer-facing work cannot create early wins.
questions.explanation: The win has to teach a behavior worth repeating. A quick measure can damage trust when it rewards the wrong habit.

questions.prompt: A logistics team calls its weekly fact review boring. The new leader sees that problems surface earlier when the review happens. How should she frame the win?
choices: She should replace the review with a more visible announcement so the win feels exciting.
She should treat the review as a temporary morale step until a larger result appears.
She should count the review as a win because it makes reality visible and repeatable.
questions.explanation: The cadence matters because it changes how the organization sees facts. Excitement is less important than a routine that exposes real work.

questions.prompt: A medical device unit has a trust problem after a safety miss. A new leader proposes a morale lunch as the first win. What is the strongest critique?
choices: The lunch may help internally, but the first win should be about faster external messaging.
The lunch should come first because people need relief before safety work can restart.
The lunch misses the test because damaged trust requires substance and accountability.
questions.explanation: In a crisis, credibility has to reach the trust problem itself. Morale can matter, but optics alone do not answer damaged safety confidence.

questions.prompt: A software firm joins a former rival's developer group and also funds shared tooling work. Which reading best fits symbolic wins?
choices: The public move can build credibility when the partnership is backed by real operating choices.
The public move is mainly a press gesture because symbols do not carry strategic value.
The public move should be hidden until all rival communities have already changed their view.
questions.explanation: A symbolic move is not shallow by default. It earns force when visible commitment lines up with real partnership and operating choices.

questions.prompt: A promoted manager says the first 90 days are just HR timing, so early moves can wait. Which response uses the transition logic?
choices: She can wait for the formal review because expectations are not stable before then.
She should act sooner because stakeholders form working assumptions during that window.
She should avoid visible moves because first impressions are too fragile to test.
questions.explanation: The window matters because people begin forming trust and expectations before formal reviews. Waiting can let others define the pattern for her.

questions.prompt: A regional head has plenty of experience and plans informal intro chats with no diagnosis notes. What should the roadmap warning change?
choices: It should make the chats longer so more people feel heard before action starts.
It should let experience replace inquiry when the business looks familiar.
It should link each chat to diagnosis and action so the meetings do not drift.
questions.explanation: Experience helps, but it does not reveal hidden constraints by itself. A roadmap keeps learning tied to choices instead of loose social calls.

questions.prompt: A retail lead can boost first-week sales by discounting every hard-to-sell item. The result would look strong. What should she check first?
choices: Whether the sales bump teaches the future behavior she wants repeated after the first week.
Whether the sales bump can be described as the largest number in the weekly update.
Whether the sales bump gives staff enough relief to delay deeper operating questions.
questions.explanation: The key test is what the win trains. A quick number can mislead if it teaches discount reflexes instead of the future operating norm.

reviewCards.front: What makes an early win build credibility instead of just noise?
reviewCards.back: It connects to the diagnosis, is visible to key stakeholders, and proves the leader can mobilize people. Speed helps only when the win teaches the right next behavior.

reviewCards.front: Why does Alan Mulally's Ford Business Plan Review count as an early win?
reviewCards.back: It changed the work rhythm. At Ford in 2006, Alan Mulally used a regular review to bring facts into the room, so the early proof was shared reality and follow-through.

reviewCards.front: What are the five checks in the Early-win screen?
reviewCards.back: The five checks are strategic relevance, visibility, behavioral signal, feasibility, and follow-through. A strong win should pass all five before it gets attention.

reviewCards.front: Why can too many first-month projects weaken momentum?
reviewCards.back: People have limited attention. When the early-win list gets crowded, stakeholders cannot tell what matters most, and the leader looks busy rather than clear.

reviewCards.front: What does STARS situation diagnosis (Ch 3) get wrong if applied naively to securing early wins?
reviewCards.back: STARS can tell you what kind of situation you are in, but it does not choose the first visible proof for you. The early win still has to teach the right behavior.

reviewCards.front: When does a visible morale win fail the credibility test?
reviewCards.back: It fails when the real issue is trust, safety, or operational accountability. In that case, the visible move has to address substance, not just lift mood.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice screening wins before you announce them. Use strategic relevance, visibility, behavioral signal, feasibility, and follow-through to cut noise. The skill is choosing proof that teaches the future way of working.

ifThenPlans.context: Your early-win list has more items than people can remember
ifThenPlans.plan: If the list starts to crowd attention, then Run the Early-Win Screen and keep only the wins whose signal a stakeholder could repeat.

ifThenPlans.context: A quick metric would improve by rewarding a bad shortcut
ifThenPlans.plan: If the number rises while the habit gets worse, then screen the win for behavioral signal before you count it as progress.

ifThenPlans.context: The useful move is a plain operating routine
ifThenPlans.plan: If the win looks too boring to announce, then screen it for visibility and follow-through. A steady cadence can still build trust.

ifThenPlans.context: The situation carries a trust or safety wound
ifThenPlans.plan: If morale work would dodge the real risk, then Run the Early-Win Screen against substance first and leave optics second.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, count every time you call a quick result a win. Mark whether it teaches a behavior you want repeated.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Across the week, tally each proposed early win under the first screen part it fails: strategic relevance, visibility, behavioral signal, feasibility, or follow-through.

memorableLines.text: A win that teaches nothing spends trust.
The best early win changes the next meeting.
Applause is not proof of progress.

chapters.title: Negotiate Success
chapters.hook: 5 boss conversations can rescue 90 days; the missed status deck only shows where drift surfaced.
chapters.counterintuition: A helpful boss can still leave the role vague: if expectations, style, resources, and development stay private, both sides grade different jobs.
chapters.tryThisNow: Put TERMS atop your notes app; during your next conversation about a mandate, replace "I'll handle it" with one question about outcomes, cadence, or resources.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Negotiate success by turning the boss relationship into explicit terms: situation, expectations, style, resources, and personal development, before assumptions harden.

breakdown.fastRead: Laura has the reply open when procurement marks two promised analysts unavailable for the month. The 90-day plan is due by morning. Her first draft looks clean, but it hides the hard parts. It lists targets without naming which work to stop, how often the boss wants updates, or what resources the plan assumes. A vague mandate becomes a private grading system. Negotiate success before the story of your performance writes itself. The move is simple: turn tasks into terms while both sides can still change them.
breakdown.deepRead:
Victoria has one individual coaching slot left in the First 90 Days work at IMD. Her draft roadmap still reads like a list of errands. She has diagnosis notes, action items, and a page of promises. Then the coach asks which boss conversation would change the first week. Victoria sees the miss. She used the First 90 Days roadmap as proof that she was organized, not as a way to set terms.

That misuse is common because a framework feels productive the moment it has boxes. The Five Conversations are not boxes to fill after the boss has already judged the work. They are five doors to open early: situation, expectations, style, resources, and personal development. Situation asks what kind of business problem you inherited. Expectations asks what success means and what not to do. Style asks how information should move. Resources asks what the plan will require. Personal development asks where the role will stretch you.

Speed without terms just makes confusion arrive sooner. If the boss wants weekly detail and you send monthly summaries, silence may read as neglect. If the boss wants quick cost action and you are still diagnosing, patience may read as drift. If you promise a full 90-day agenda before you name the resources, the gap becomes a credibility problem. Terms Before Tasks means replacing the reflex to accept the assignment with a small negotiation about the assignment's shape.
breakdown.fullRead:
A Microsoft promotion shows why this is not only for outsiders. Satya Nadella already knew much of the company before taking the top role, yet the move still required a higher-altitude mandate. Familiar names and old wins do not automatically answer what the new role must protect, change, fund, or stop.

That is the hard edge of negotiating success. It is not asking the boss to make the job easy. It is asking enough direct questions that both of you can judge progress by the same terms. The boss relationship is part of the transition system. It is not background weather.

Start with the situation conversation. Is the unit in start-up, turnaround, accelerated growth, realignment, or sustaining success mode? The exact labels matter less than the shared read. A boss who sees a crisis will judge slow listening differently from a boss who sees a healthy team needing care.

Then move to expectations. Many new leaders stop too early here. They ask for targets and miss the negative space. What should not be done? Which inherited commitments are off-limits? Which visible win would be hollow? A boss may say "grow the business" while also expecting no disruption to a fragile customer base. Those two facts belong in the same conversation.

Style comes next because daily contact creates daily meaning. Some bosses want detail because they are anxious. Some want detail because the risk is real. Some want exception reports and will read long updates as noise. The leader who leaves cadence implicit invites small messages to carry large meanings. One unanswered note can become a story about trust.

Resources negotiated late become promises broken in public. A plan that needs analysts, budget, access, or decision rights should say so before the leader commits to the full 90-day agenda. This is not whining. It is capacity math. A blown deadline often begins as a brave yes in a room where nobody named the missing file, person, or approval.

Personal development may feel like the softest conversation, but it often carries the sharpest risk. The new role may demand enterprise judgment, board communication, or work across groups that used to be peers. IMD's First 90 Days work includes individual coaching because transition practice needs rehearsal, not only intent.

Use Terms Before Tasks when a request sounds clear but the terms around it are not. Ask what success will mean, what tradeoffs are allowed, how the boss wants to work, what the plan requires, and where you need coaching. This advice misleads a boss who wants obedience more than alignment; that person hears negotiation as resistance, not as shared discipline.

examples.title: The Hidden Terms Call
examples.scenario: Laura has the reply open in her home office when procurement marks two promised analysts unavailable for the month. The board wants the 90-day plan by morning. As the new operations lead, she sees her First 90 Days worksheet from IMD has become a slide checklist, not a negotiation. Laura must choose which cost to own: send neat targets with no resources named, or ask for a call and risk looking slow before trust is built.
examples.whatToDo: Laura asks for a terms call before sending the deck. She names the target, the work she would stop, and the people the plan assumes are available.
examples.whyItMatters: The method fails when it becomes proof of diligence. It works when Laura uses it to make the success contract visible before the boss grades the plan.

examples.title: The Coaching Slot
examples.scenario: After the 3 half days, the individual coaching slot is nearly gone, and Victoria's transition roadmap still has no boss agreement on it. She stops filling boxes and says, "I made the program into homework." Gilles says, "Then it is not a roadmap. Which boss conversation changes tomorrow?" "Resources," she says. "I promised the plan before I named the people."
examples.whatToDo: Victoria moves one item from the roadmap into tomorrow's boss agenda. She changes the line from a task she will complete to a resource term she must settle.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange turns coaching into practice. A roadmap helps only when it changes the next conversation, not when it becomes a tidy record of private effort.

examples.title: The Quiet Style Gap
examples.scenario: The style part of First 90 Days work at IMD sounds easy until Fabienne drafts her update: customers, cloud spend, hiring, product risk. She expects old credibility to carry the meeting. The reveal comes in her boss's margin note: "Too much detail, no escalation rule." She knew the work, but not the new style.
examples.whatToDo: Fabienne rewrites the update as three rules: what she will send weekly, what she will escalate the same day, and what detail she will keep out unless asked.
examples.whyItMatters: Internal knowledge can hide a fresh contract. Style is not personality polish; it controls information flow and how fast decisions can move.

examples.title: The Text That Stops
examples.scenario:
"She wants details every hour," someone says, and Gilles deletes the long update he had drafted after individual coaching in the 3 half days. The vendor-access form locks in ten minutes, and the gate agent has started boarding.
Boss: "Status?"
Gilles: "Green except vendor access. Escalate now or in weekly note?"
Boss: "Now if access blocks launch. Weekly if it is noise."
Gilles: "Using that rule."
examples.whatToDo: Gilles turns the exchange into a written cadence rule. He separates same-day escalation from routine updates before the next travel gap can distort the silence.
examples.whyItMatters: The short thread makes style operational. Without a cadence rule, a dead phone or delayed reply can look like avoidance instead of a normal constraint.

examples.title: The Plan Restart
examples.scenario: "Ship the 90-day plan without asking for more headcount," the boss says, and Brenda's pen stops on the front stoop.
