She has been using the First 90 Days frame from IMD as a private checklist. This time she turns to a fresh page and writes three columns: target, owner, resource gap.
examples.whatToDo: Brenda restarts the call around capacity. She accepts the outcome only after naming which target needs an owner, which one needs access, and which one should wait.
examples.whyItMatters: The pause is the skill. Resource gaps found late make the leader look undisciplined, even when the real failure was an under-specified promise.

examples.title: The Blank Coaching Line
examples.scenario: The pen rolls under Alexis's notebook during individual coaching after the 3 half days, leaving the last line blank: personal development. She has already written situation, expectations, style, and resources because those topics felt easier to defend. The blank space is small, but it is the only one her boss cannot guess for her.
examples.whatToDo: She adds one plain line about finance practice, then writes a boss request beside it: which meetings will teach the judgment the new role requires.
examples.whyItMatters: The quiet line protects the transition from private pretending. A stretch role needs coaching terms as much as it needs targets.

questions.prompt: A notes file has five headings, but only the performance target heading has anything under it. Which repair best matches boss alignment?
choices: Add more detail under the target heading so the boss can judge progress with less follow-up.
Fill in situation, expectations, style, resources, and personal development so hidden assumptions surface.
Move the target heading to the top so the plan starts with the clearest business outcome.
questions.explanation: The Five Conversations are the full frame. Targets alone leave the situation, working style, resources, and development needs implicit, which creates hidden risk.

questions.prompt: A leader sends long updates that the boss skims, then sends short updates the boss reads as neglect. Which topic needs to be negotiated?
choices: The leader should revisit the business situation because the updates may be reporting the wrong risks.
The leader should revisit personal development because the updates may reveal a weak executive voice.
The leader should set cadence, detail level, and escalation norms because style is affecting information flow.
questions.explanation: The source fact names cadence, detail, and escalation as working style issues. The problem is not just tone; the communication system is undefined.

questions.prompt: A draft agenda commits to a full 90-day push before anyone names budget, staff time, or access rights. Where is the first defect?
choices: The agenda lacks a personal development item that would show where the leader needs coaching.
The agenda accepts commitments before resource gaps are negotiated with the boss.
The agenda overuses diagnosis when a strong leader should move faster into delivery.
questions.explanation: Resources should be negotiated before the leader commits to the full agenda. Otherwise the plan creates credibility risk when capacity fails later.

questions.prompt: A transition roadmap has diagnosis notes and action items, but every boss meeting remains a loose check-in. What should change?
choices: Use the roadmap to connect diagnosis to concrete boss agreements, not only to organize private notes.
Use the roadmap mainly to show experience, since senior leaders need less inquiry in a new role.
Use the roadmap as a social map, since early meetings should avoid structured business questions.
questions.explanation: IMD presents the roadmap as diagnosis linked to action planning. If meetings stay loose, the roadmap is not shaping the transition.

questions.prompt: A program combines structured transition work with individual coaching. Why does that structure fit boss alignment work?
choices: It protects the leader from political conversations by keeping the work inside private preparation.
It gives the leader space to test expectations and make assumptions discussable instead of guessed.
It replaces the need for boss conversations by making the transition method formal enough on its own.
questions.explanation: Coaching supports explicit negotiation. The structure does not avoid politics or replace boss talks; it makes the assumptions safer to discuss.

questions.prompt: A manager says the first 90 days are just an HR onboarding period and plans to clarify terms after the first review. Which reading fits Negotiate Success?
choices: The early window matters because stakeholders form working assumptions before formal reviews occur.
The early window matters mainly because HR needs a standard period for role paperwork.
The early window matters only after targets are missed and the boss asks for a reset.
questions.explanation: The 90-day window matters because trust and expectations form early. Waiting for the first review lets private assumptions harden.

questions.prompt: A boss gives clear revenue targets but never discusses the inherited situation or the leader's development needs. What is still exposed?
choices: The transition contract still has hidden assumptions because the full set of boss conversations is incomplete.
The transition contract is mostly complete because performance targets are the strongest boss signal.
The transition contract should shift toward informal trust because formal topics may slow the relationship.
questions.explanation: The Five Conversations frame does not reduce boss alignment to targets. Omitting situation, style, resources, or development leaves assumptions in the contract.

questions.prompt: A veteran leader argues that a roadmap is unnecessary because experience already provides pattern recognition. Which answer best follows the source?
choices: Experience should replace structured inquiry when the leader has handled similar roles before.
Experience should narrow the inquiry to only the areas where the leader feels least certain.
Experience can help, but it cannot reveal a new role's hidden constraints without inquiry.
questions.explanation: The roadmap is not for beginners only. Experience can speed recognition, but the new role still has constraints that must be discovered.

questions.prompt: A team misses a deadline after the new leader promised a larger agenda than the staff could carry. Which earlier move would have reduced the risk?
choices: The leader should have increased the status-report detail before the deadline exposed the gap.
The leader should have delayed diagnosis until the team had delivered one visible early win.
The leader should have negotiated resources before turning the agenda into public commitments.
questions.explanation: The source fact ties late resource discovery to credibility risk. More reporting would not fix a promise made beyond capacity.

reviewCards.front: What are the Five Conversations a new leader should have with the boss?
reviewCards.back: They are situation, expectations, style, resources, and personal development. Together they turn the boss relationship from private guessing into shared terms for the transition.

reviewCards.front: Why is working style more than a personality issue in boss-alignment work?
reviewCards.back: Style sets cadence, detail level, and escalation norms. When those are hidden, the boss may read the same update as mistrust, neglect, or noise.

reviewCards.front: Why should resources be negotiated before a full 90-day agenda is promised?
reviewCards.back: Commitments consume capacity. If the leader discovers missing staff, budget, access, or decision rights after promising the agenda, ambition becomes credibility risk.

reviewCards.front: How does coaching support boss alignment rather than replace it?
reviewCards.back: Coaching lets the leader try the wording before the real boss conversation. The boss terms still have to be negotiated with the boss.

reviewCards.front: How does learning before acting show up in Victoria's coaching slot?
reviewCards.back: Victoria stops using the roadmap as private homework. She turns one finding into the next resource conversation, so learning changes the boss agreement before work starts.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice replacing a quick yes with a short terms check. Before you accept a new mandate, ask which situation you are entering, what success means, how the boss wants information, what resources the plan assumes, and where the role will stretch you.

ifThenPlans.context: A new assignment sounds clear because the outcome has a number attached.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a target arrives without terms, then ask which of the Five Conversations is still missing before you commit to the work.

ifThenPlans.context: A boss reacts oddly to an update that seemed normal to you.
ifThenPlans.plan: If an update creates friction, then ask for the preferred cadence, detail level, and escalation line before sending the next one.

ifThenPlans.context: A plan requires people, access, or budget you do not control.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the agenda depends on capacity outside your control, then name the resource gap before the promise becomes public.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Put a small question mark beside your mandate notes. During your next conversation about a mandate, mark one missing term before you agree to the next task.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one workweek, swap your default quick yes for Terms Before Tasks on the first new request each day. Compare the first half of the week with the second: which boss terms got clearer, and which still stayed vague?

memorableLines.text: A vague mandate becomes a private grading system.
Speed without terms just makes confusion arrive sooner.
Resources negotiated late become promises broken in public.

chapters.title: Achieve Alignment
chapters.hook: A brand brief crosses three desks and loses the strategy it was meant to carry.
chapters.counterintuition: What looks like resistance is actually good people obeying the system around them. If the old metrics, roles, and culture point left, a speech about going right will not carry the work.
chapters.tryThisNow: With your first coffee, notice one place work pulls against itself. Count four slow breaths, then write the exact question you will ask about the mismatch.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Alignment means making strategy, structure, systems, skills, and culture teach the same behavior; fix the few mismatches that block execution before you blame people.

breakdown.fastRead:
A brand brief leaves one agency with a sharp promise, then returns with three different voices. One team sells speed. Another sells safety. A third sells low price. The work is not sloppy; the system is split. Misfit makes good people look stubborn.

You see the same drag when a new plan rewards one behavior while the old meeting, metric, or approval path rewards another. Organizational alignment means strategy, structure, systems, skills, and culture all push the same way. People follow the system they are in. Before you fault the team, ask which part of the setup is still teaching the past.
breakdown.deepRead:
The gear that does the damage is simple: every workplace teaches by reward. The poster says one thing, the bonus says another, and the weekly meeting settles the fight. Strategy is the aim. Structure is who owns what. Systems are the routines and measures. Skills are the work people can perform. Culture is what people learn is safe here.

The IBM consolidation of many ad agencies in the 1990s makes the point. A common brand message could not live as a slogan while every unit bought its own voice. The message needed a structure and a supplier choice that made one IBM easier to say. A reorg is not alignment. It is only one piece of the design.

IMD gives the same idea a classroom shape. Leaders move from diagnosis to action planning instead of leaving with loose advice. That format matters because the leader does not just hear advice. The leader is pressed to plan the next talk before the old calendar eats the week. Plans need places to live.

For you, the test is plain. When work drags, do not ask first who lacks will. Ask what the current setup pays, hides, slows, or protects. Then pick the mismatch that blocks execution now, not the one that simply annoys you most.
breakdown.fullRead:
Sadie's marker stops over Ogilvy & Mather, and the pause is the lesson. The IBM brand problem looks like a message problem, so the expert answer is tempting: consolidate the agencies and make the market hear one IBM. Then Sadie catches herself. She can solve the voice problem and still leave the work split underneath it.

That is where alignment becomes more than neat design. Strategy names the direction. Structure decides who owns pieces of the work. Systems set the measures, meetings, budgets, and approvals. Skills decide what people can do without faking it. Culture tells people what is safe, admired, and punished when the boss is not in the room.

A leader in the first 90 days has to read those parts as a set. If the strategy says one customer experience, but regional teams keep separate agencies, the message breaks. If the structure says shared platform, but pay still rewards local wins, the old habit survives. If culture says candor, but bad news gets buried in replies, silence wins.

IBM's move to Ogilvy & Mather is memorable because it joined the outside voice to the inside need. The company needed to seem less fragmented and act less fragmented. A common brand voice could help only if leaders also asked where the old split still lived in roles, measures, and choices. Words travel farther when work backs them.

IMD's program gives this work a practical shape. The learning design keeps the leader from drifting through vague meetings. Case work then brings the general method back to the leader's own role. Which expectation is unclear? Which team role is wrong? Which alliance is missing? Which early win sits on a weak system?

The order matters. If you change culture language first, but the skill gap remains, people may agree and still fail. If you train skills first, but decision rights stay stuck, trained people may wait for permission. Each repair asks what the next part of the design must do so the first repair can hold.

The first 90 days also limit how much repair you can ask people to absorb. A leader who opens every mismatch at once creates fog. A leader who changes boxes before diagnosis burns trust. A sound sequence names the target behavior, traces the few blocks that stop it, and explains the order before people invent their own story.

There is a counter-case. Clifford runs a tiny support desk where the strategy is clear, the roles are clean, and one client has a broken account before renewal. If Clifford pauses to map all five design parts before approving the fix, he has obeyed the idea badly. Alignment should not become a delay costume. When the path is clear and the cost is live, do the work first and study the pattern after.

examples.title: Ogilvy Limit
examples.scenario: Sadie is circling Ogilvy & Mather on the agency map while the IBM brand deck is still open. She tells James, "One voice solves the problem," then stops with the marker in the air. "No. I know the message problem, not the operating problem." The room waits because Sadie is the expert, and she has just named the edge of her expertise.
examples.whatToDo: Sadie changes the question in the room. She asks which metrics, approvals, and local habits would still pull IBM units away from one brand message.
examples.whyItMatters: The admission keeps the fix honest. A leader can know the visible problem and still need a wider check before declaring the system aligned.

examples.title: Stuck Memo
examples.scenario: Clifford's binder clip snaps against his thumb as the IMD draft memo refuses to lie flat. The first line reads: "Do not let the First 90 Days become a welcome talk." The memo proposes 3 half days, then pairs individual coaching with expectations, team choices, alliances, and early wins. A margin reply asks, "Where does alignment get practiced?"
examples.whatToDo: Clifford edits the memo so each teaching block ends with a written alignment check, not a loose reflection. The program now makes leaders draft the next conversation.
examples.whyItMatters: A roadmap has to change the learner's next move. The memo turns transition advice into a place where diagnosis and action meet.

examples.title: Two Launch Paths
examples.scenario: Launch lead James hears the Slack chime under the espresso grinder in a coworking lounge before standup. IBM and Ogilvy & Mather sit at the top of the brand thread. He treats the missed support message as noise and asks the team to push harder. Cheryl reads the same thread, asks why the reward system says the opposite, and pauses until sales and support agree on the signal.
examples.whatToDo: Cheryl uses the missed message as evidence of misfit. She ties the launch talk to the metric and handoff that will shape daily behavior.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows why effort is not enough. The same strategy lands differently when one leader pushes words and another repairs the signal.

examples.title: Marker Cap Coach
examples.scenario: Mathilde rolls the marker cap between two fingers before writing culture under IBM's 1990s move to Ogilvy & Mather. "One agency helped the voice," she tells the coach. "What if the units still buy their own habits?" The coach says, "If the work teaches the old rule, your speech cannot teach the new one."
examples.whatToDo: Mathilde maps strategy, structure, systems, skills, and culture beside the candor goal. She picks the reply norm as the first mismatch to change.
examples.whyItMatters: The coach talk makes culture concrete. A leader changes what people learn by changing what the work rewards, permits, and repeats.

examples.title: Agency Case Confusion
examples.scenario: Ellie erases the last agency arrow while the case class is still debating IBM's 1990s move to Ogilvy & Mather. "So alignment means pick the cleanest supplier?" she asks. The coach points back to the split units. "No. It means learn which mismatches will block the common message, then sequence the repair."
examples.whatToDo: Ellie rewrites her class plan around the one mismatch most likely to block early wins. She saves the rest for coaching, not the first push.
examples.whyItMatters: The confusion is useful because many leaders overfill the first months. Alignment narrows attention to the blocks that matter soonest.

examples.title: Agency Route Repair
examples.scenario: Operations lead Emile is updating the IBM agency list at the brand operations desk when a local request interrupts the 1990s consolidation log. Last month, the request bounced among old agencies and came back with three voices. This week, the same request routes to Ogilvy & Mather first, and the draft returns with one message before the market window closes.
examples.whatToDo: Emile changes the routing rule to match the common brand goal. The process now sends the work through the same path the strategy needs.
examples.whyItMatters: The before-and-after makes alignment visible. One changed system can turn a common message from wishful wording into daily practice.

questions.prompt: A new operations head removes diagnosis meetings from her entry plan and calls the first 90 days a quiet settling-in period. Which read fits the transition risk?
choices: The period mainly gives HR enough time to finish entry paperwork.
The period shapes trust and expectations before later room to maneuver is set.
The period matters only after the first formal review is scheduled.
questions.explanation: Early moves teach stakeholders what to expect. Treating the window as paperwork misses how fast working assumptions form.

questions.prompt: A senior hire says her long experience makes a transition roadmap unnecessary. Which response best fits the source logic?
choices: A roadmap should be skipped when experience already gives enough pattern recognition.
A roadmap still matters because the new role has hidden constraints to learn.
A roadmap should focus on introductions instead of diagnosis and action planning.
questions.explanation: Experience can speed learning, but it does not reveal the new role's constraints by itself. The roadmap links inquiry to action.

questions.prompt: A brand group keeps separate agency contracts while asking the market to hear one company voice. IBM's Ogilvy move points to which correction?
choices: Agency choice should stay separate so brand teams can move without strategy work.
Agency choice matters only after internal structure and systems are already perfect.
Agency choice can support strategy when a common message reduces fragmentation.
questions.explanation: The IBM case links external message to strategic coherence. Branding is not separate when fragmented messages teach fragmented behavior.

questions.prompt: A log shows the new strategy changed the org chart, yet incentives and culture still reward the old behavior. What should the leader infer?
choices: The reorg handled structure, but other design elements still teach the old rule.
The reorg proves alignment is complete once reporting lines are cleaner.
The reorg should be repeated until every box matches the strategy wording.
questions.explanation: Structure is only one element. Systems and culture can keep old behavior alive even after reporting lines change.

questions.prompt: A division redraws reporting lines, sends the new chart, and expects culture to change by Friday. Which answer best reads the gap?
choices: The structure should stay symbolic until the culture changes on its own.
The structure should replace systems work because people need clearer boxes first.
The structure needs matching systems, skills, and culture to shift behavior.
questions.explanation: Structure is only one part of the architecture. Systems, skills, and culture can keep teaching the old behavior after boxes move.

questions.prompt: A dashboard shows early wins planned before expectation talks, team choices, or alliance work. Which risk should stand out?
choices: The wins may fail because related moves are already pulling against them.
The wins should be isolated so the team can avoid stakeholder pressure.
The wins can wait until alignment has been solved across every unit.
questions.explanation: Expectation, team, alliance, and early-win work interact. A win can stall when systems or stakeholders pull the other way.

questions.prompt: A new leader lists many mismatches on entry day and wants to repair all of them at once. Which next move fits alignment work?
choices: Repair the easiest mismatches first so the team sees visible activity.
Open every mismatch at once so no group feels left out of the transition.
Pick the few bottlenecks that block execution and sequence those repairs.
questions.explanation: Alignment work needs focus. Trying to fix every mismatch at once overloads the transition and blurs priority.

questions.prompt: A colleague skims a transition agenda and calls First 90 Days advice generic onboarding. Which evidence best corrects that read?
choices: The method can be treated as informal advice when a leader already has a strong network.
IMD links the work to Michael Watkins's transition teaching and program leadership.
The advice matters mainly because many companies use onboarding checklists.
questions.explanation: The IMD link ties the method to named transition research and teaching. It is not just loose career advice.

questions.prompt: A manager studies a team that says yes to strategy but keeps missing handoffs. Which diagnostic pass should come first?
choices: Check strategy, structure, systems, skills, and culture for the signal each one sends.
Announce the strategy again so people cannot claim they missed the message.
Move the team under a new manager before checking routines or skills.
questions.explanation: The full architecture matters because each part teaches behavior. Repeating the message or moving boxes may miss the actual drag.

reviewCards.front: What are the five parts of organizational architecture to check for alignment?
reviewCards.back: Check strategy, structure, systems, skills, and culture. Each one teaches people what behavior is safe, rewarded, possible, or slow.

reviewCards.front: Why did IBM's move to Ogilvy & Mather count as more than a branding choice?
reviewCards.back: It joined external message to strategic coherence. A common brand voice helped IBM act less fragmented instead of leaving each unit to signal its own direction.

reviewCards.front: Why should a new leader fix only a few alignment mismatches first?
reviewCards.back: The first 90 days can overload fast. Picking the few blocks that stop execution makes change feel tied to strategy, not like random disruption.

reviewCards.front: Which matters more here, role-break discipline (Ch 1) or organizational alignment, and why?
reviewCards.back: Role-break discipline gets you out of old personal habits. Organizational alignment matters more once the system itself keeps rewarding old behavior.

reviewCards.front: Why is a mission statement too weak by itself to change culture?
reviewCards.back: A mission can point the way, but culture changes when systems, partnerships, and leader behavior repeat the same signal in daily work.

reviewCards.front: What connected moves does IMD tie to First 90 Days work?
reviewCards.back: It links aligning expectations, reshaping teams, creating alliances, and securing early wins. Those moves interact, so one isolated fix can drag against another.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use Map the Mismatch Before You Move when execution drag appears. Name the target behavior, then check strategy, structure, systems, skills, and culture for the signal each one sends. Pick the mismatch that blocks work now.

ifThenPlans.context: If a team agrees with the strategy but keeps doing the old work.
ifThenPlans.plan: If agreement does not change behavior, then map the mismatch before you move. Write what each design part is teaching today.

ifThenPlans.context: If the mismatch list starts to sprawl.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the list gets long, then circle the one block that slows execution this week. Leave the rest visible but out of the first repair.

ifThenPlans.context: If a message sounds clean but behavior stays split.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the words travel better than the work, then check the structure and system behind the message before sending another version.

ifThenPlans.context: If an early win depends on people who have not been brought in.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the win needs other owners, then map the stakeholder pull before you move. Ask which alliance or expectation talk is missing.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, choose one work mismatch and pre-write the words for your next ask: "I see us saying X while the system rewards Y. Can we change Z first?"
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, teach Map the Mismatch Before You Move to one person in your own words. Use one real mismatch and ask them to name the design part you missed.

memorableLines.text: Misfit makes good people look stubborn.
A reorg is not alignment.
Words travel farther when work backs them.

chapters.title: Build Your Team
chapters.hook: 5 lenses can find the role problem a loyal hunch keeps missing.
chapters.counterintuition: A team can feel loyal and still be built for yesterday's work. You can respect the people you inherit and still test whether the roles fit the work now.
chapters.tryThisNow: Within the next 24 hours, the first time you open your laptop for team work, spend 10 minutes naming one role through the five lenses.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Build the inherited team by testing competence, judgment, energy, trust, and role fit before you protect the roster or start replacing people.

breakdown.fastRead: Why does Ava hesitate with the roster open and a missed handoff blinking in the project log? The easy story is about one weak person. The useful question is sharper: is the person weak, or is the role unclear? Build Your Team is about team architecture, the human system you inherit when you take a new role. You look at competence, judgment, energy, trust, and role fit before you decide who stays, who moves, and what cadence changes first. Private hunches make poor team architecture.
breakdown.deepRead:
The mechanism is simple: a team shows its truth when work has a rhythm and facts have somewhere to land. A new leader who only holds private chats may hear charm, fear, or old loyalty. A repeated operating review lets the same people face the same facts more than once. Patterns appear. Who names risk early? Who hides bad news until it is polite? Who has skill but no clear lane?

That is why the five lenses matter. Competence asks if the person can do the work. Judgment asks how the person chooses when the map is messy. Energy asks whether the person can carry the pace. Trust asks whether others can rely on the person with hard facts. Role fit asks whether the role now demands a different shape. Cadence turns opinion into evidence.

A crisis-entry lens adds the harder warning. A leader can know the company and still need to relearn where truth gets stuck. Familiar faces do not prove that safety risks, customer pain, or weak accountability will surface. In your own first 90 days, the same risk is smaller but real. A skipped check-in becomes a buried warning. A buried warning becomes a dropped opportunity, such as the referral Jade meant to answer before the window closed. The team may not need a purge. It may need clearer roles, a new meeting rhythm, and one fast decision where the role is too critical to drift.
breakdown.fullRead:
A reception desk can teach the whole chapter if the line keeps forming in the wrong place. Renee sees the same delay each morning. One person looks slow, so the old manager would have coached her again. Renee waits long enough to watch the handoff. The intake worker is covering two decisions that should belong to different roles. If Renee replaces her, the jam survives with a new name tag.

This is the part of team building that feels unfair at first. You are judging people before you know them well. The answer is not to pretend you know nothing. The answer is to gather better evidence than mood. Use the First 90 Days idea as a roadmap, not as a social tour. Ask what the role is for, what standard matters now, and what proof would change your mind.

The IMD framing of transition work helps because it links diagnosis to action. Meetings are not visits to make people comfortable. They are a way to learn where the system is strong, where the process is broken, and where a person is blocking a critical role. If every meeting ends with warmer feelings and no clearer choices, the team has only learned your manners.

The fair move is slower in some places and faster in others. Slow down when early performance is tangled with vague roles, broken cadence, or missing information. Speed up when a critical role keeps blocking the transition agenda. Mercy is not drift in a critical role. Tell people which standard is changing before you judge their response to it. That sentence sounds basic, but it is where many transitions lose trust.

The overcorrection is a leader who turns assessment into surveillance. Every pause becomes a clue. Every mistake becomes a file note. People stop telling the truth because the new leader seems to be building a case, not building a team. That version of rigor curdles into fear. The better standard is open evidence: clear roles, visible facts, repeated forums, and direct coaching before final calls where coaching can still help.

You are not building a perfect roster in 90 days. You are building enough truth to act. Some people will rise when the role is clarified. Some will need a different seat. A few will need to leave sooner because the work cannot wait. Ava's opening question resolves here: do not ask first whether the person disappoints you. Ask what the role requires, what the evidence shows, and what delay now costs the rest of the team.

examples.title: Roster Thought Loop
examples.scenario: The roster has no empty seats, yet the handoffs keep landing late. At 7:40 a.m., Ava stands by the reception desk as the new team lead, with the IMD First 90 Days roadmap in mind. The old answer comes first: replace the coordinator. Then the wrong turn catches. Maybe skill is not the first lens. Competence looks decent. Judgment looks careful. Energy is low, but only after the intake role swallows two jobs. Trust is fraying because role fit is bad.
examples.whatToDo: Ava marks the role through competence, judgment, energy, trust, and role fit before asking for a personnel change or a public correction.
examples.whyItMatters: The first read protects her from blaming a person for a bad design. A team can need clearer architecture before it needs a new name on the roster.

examples.title: Closed Referral Window
examples.scenario: The referral window closed while the inbox still looked tidy. Fleur records a voice memo before touching the next plan, because the IMD First 90 Days roadmap warns her that hard team truths can hide inside a cleaner dashboard. She has only a few early meetings to spend. Finance wants one. The field team wants one. The quiet risk review wants one. Her old rule says follow the biggest number first; this exception says hidden harm may not arrive as a big number.
examples.whatToDo: Fleur gives the quiet risk review a slot in the first learning cycle and names which trust signal she needs from each meeting.
examples.whyItMatters: Scarce attention is a team choice. If hidden risk gets no early forum, the leader may protect the visible plan while the real damage grows.

examples.title: Critical Seat Call
examples.scenario: "Keep her in the role through the quarter," the board liaison says, and Renee hears both bad options. The IMD First 90 Days roadmap says team building cannot wait, but local knowledge still matters. If Renee moves the operations lead now, knowledge leaves during a fragile handoff. If she waits, the transition agenda stays blocked behind missed calls and slow decisions. Equal time for every role would look fair and work unfairly.
examples.whatToDo: Renee gives the role one direct standard, one short evidence window, and a named backup plan if the bottleneck remains after coaching.
examples.whyItMatters: Fairness includes the weight of the role. A peripheral mismatch can take more coaching time; a critical mismatch can tax everyone by noon.

examples.title: Review Rhythm Talk
examples.scenario:
The clean dashboard sits on Jade's tablet; the messy call notes sit on Renee's lap. Both are true.

Jade says, "The dashboard says green."

Renee says, "Use the Ford 2006 cadence rule. Same facts, same weekday."

"That feels heavy."

"Only if the color was hiding the work. A scale feels heavy when people prefer guessing."
examples.whatToDo: Jade keeps the review short but repeated: same priorities, same facts, same room for bad news before rescue plans begin.
examples.whyItMatters: A cadence shows reliability under pressure. It can reveal who tells the truth early and who manages the room instead of the work.

examples.title: Clipboard Roadmap
examples.scenario: The senior pharmacist is out sick, and Lily, three days into the role, gets the intake clipboard. Everyone expects her to spend the first week being agreeable. The reveal comes by Friday: the warmest meetings taught her almost nothing, while the IMD First 90 Days roadmap exposed two role gaps and one decision rule nobody owned. The friendly path felt safe; the roadmap made the team legible.
examples.whatToDo: Lily turns each intake meeting into one diagnosis note and one action question, so goodwill does not replace evidence or delay a role call.
examples.whyItMatters: Experience helps, but a roadmap keeps the first 90 days from becoming a tour. Team building belongs in the entry plan, not the second year.

examples.title: Thread Before Send
examples.scenario:
Vivian is deleting the sentence "I think we need to replace him" while the reply bubble is still moving. At 6:20 p.m. on the living-room couch, the team manager keeps the thread open.

Vivian: The numbers are late again.

Ava: Skill or role fit?

Vivian: I only checked skill.

Ava: The Ford 2006 lesson was cadence before verdicts.

Vivian: So test judgment, not hours?

Ava: Yes. Make the role visible first.

Vivian's thumb stops over send.
examples.whatToDo: Vivian rewrites the message as an evidence request: what judgment the role needs, where delay appears, and what support has already been tried.
examples.whyItMatters: The thread keeps one early frustration from becoming a verdict. A weak result may call for a role reset before a replacement.

questions.prompt: A log shows repeated late handoffs after a new routing rule changed who owns approvals. Which read should come first?
choices: Check whether role confusion is making capable people look weak.
Assume the person with the latest handoffs lacks the needed skill.
Wait until the formal review period proves whether talent is missing.
questions.explanation: The fact says role confusion can mimic poor talent. The tempting skill read moves too fast when the process changed first.

questions.prompt: A leader sees one mismatch in a core decision role and another in a low-impact support role. How should timing differ?
choices: Give both roles the same long runway so the process feels even.
Move faster on the core role because delay spreads through the team.
Delay both calls until every inherited role has been reviewed.
questions.explanation: Critical-role misfit carries wider cost. Equal time can look fair while letting one blocking role slow the transition.

questions.prompt: A team gives polished one-on-one updates, but no one has seen how they handle bad facts together. What would add useful evidence?
choices: Ask for longer private updates from the people who seem most loyal.
Make an early roster call before the group learns the new standard.
Create a repeated forum where the same facts are visible each time.
questions.explanation: A repeated cadence reveals behavior under pressure. Private impressions alone can miss how the team handles shared facts.

questions.prompt: Jade has worked inside the company for years and now leads it from a higher seat. What should she still test?
choices: Whether familiar people should be trusted without a fresh review.
Whether prior relationships can replace the learning agenda.
Whether accountability changes when the mandate and role change.
questions.explanation: Internal knowledge helps, but a new mandate changes what the leader needs from the team. Familiarity is not full assessment.

questions.prompt: Vivian says team reshaping can wait until next year because the first months are only for orientation. Which reply fits the source idea?
choices: Wait if the team seems friendly, because trust should precede team changes.
Start team building in the transition roadmap because unresolved issues consume capacity now.
Focus only on personal credibility until the first annual review is complete.
questions.explanation: The source frames team building as a core transition task. Waiting treats a live capacity drain as later maintenance.

questions.prompt: A skilled leader plans a week of friendly intro meetings with no written diagnosis or next action. What is missing?
choices: A roadmap that connects what she learns to what she will do next.
A lighter schedule that leaves diagnosis until experience takes over.
A confidence check that keeps action planning out of early meetings.
questions.explanation: The roadmap links diagnosis to action. Experience may help, but it does not uncover hidden constraints by itself.

questions.prompt: A new leader treats the first 90 days as paperwork before the real job starts. What has she underestimated?
choices: People form working assumptions before the formal review arrives.
The period matters only because HR records need a clean date.
The first months are too early for team expectations to matter.
questions.explanation: The early window shapes trust and room to maneuver. The HR-only reading misses how quickly people set expectations.

questions.prompt: A service team misses targets after two reporting lines were merged. What should Lily sort before replacing anyone?
choices: Whether the weakest week proves the team lacks basic ability.
Whether the merged role has blurred ownership and distorted performance.
Whether waiting for perfect data would avoid a hard personnel call.
questions.explanation: Role ambiguity can distort capability. The right move asks for evidence before reading weak early output as weak talent.

questions.prompt: A blocker sits in the role that owns the transition agenda. What makes a faster call fair rather than rash?
choices: The leader wants visible toughness before the team settles.
Every inherited person deserves the same amount of time.
The role's impact makes delay costly for the wider system.
questions.explanation: Fairness includes role importance. Moving faster is justified by system cost, not by impatience or a wish to look tough.

reviewCards.front: What are the five lenses for assessing an inherited team?
reviewCards.back: Use competence, judgment, energy, trust, and role fit. The list keeps you from collapsing every weak result into a talent problem.

reviewCards.front: How does a repeated review cadence improve team assessment?
reviewCards.back: It lets the same people face the same facts more than once. That rhythm shows who names risk, who hides it, and who can work with visible reality.

reviewCards.front: Why is early weak performance not always a talent verdict?
reviewCards.back: Broken process and unclear roles can make capable people look weak. Before replacing someone, test whether the job shape is distorting the result.

reviewCards.front: How would you restate credibility-building wins (Ch 4), then use that idea on this team's problem?
reviewCards.back: A good early win proves you understand the situation and can mobilize people. For team building, the win is not a flashy firing; it is one clear role reset backed by evidence.

reviewCards.front: When should a leader move faster on role fit?
reviewCards.back: Move faster when the misfit sits in a critical role and blocks the transition agenda. Fairness includes the cost that delay pushes onto everyone else.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice reading a team through five lenses before you make a people call. Check competence, judgment, energy, trust, and role fit, then ask whether the evidence points to coaching, role clarity, cadence, or replacement.

ifThenPlans.context: If one person looks weak right after a process or role change
ifThenPlans.plan: If one person looks weak after the work changed, then run the Five-Lens Team Check before naming talent as the cause.

ifThenPlans.context: If private impressions are starting to harden into a roster story
ifThenPlans.plan: If private impressions are hardening, then create one repeated fact forum so the team can show behavior in the open.

ifThenPlans.context: If a critical role keeps slowing the transition agenda
ifThenPlans.plan: If a critical role keeps blocking the work, then set one clear standard and a short evidence window before the next call.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time you touch your laptop lid before a team decision, write one role name and score it through the five lenses.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Run the Five-Lens Team Check three times this week at widening gaps: first on an obvious role, later on a mixed case, and finally on the role you most want to avoid.

memorableLines.text: Private hunches make poor team architecture.
Cadence turns opinion into evidence.
Mercy is not drift in a critical role.

chapters.title: Create Alliances
chapters.hook: I used to start with the org chart. What if the real vote sits outside your line?
chapters.counterintuition: Despite the comfort of a title, your plan often moves only after people outside your line decide it helps them too.
chapters.tryThisNow: When your next reply is ready to send, put your calendar beside the draft, move one stakeholder conversation earlier, and rehearse the ask once.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Map who can help or block the work, learn what each person needs, and build support in an order that makes the next yes easier.

breakdown.fastRead: A missed ally does not usually announce itself. You find out when the budget signer goes quiet, the lead engineer will not commit, or the partner who could have made the plan credible has chosen someone else. Create Alliances starts with that cost. Authority opens doors; alliances move work. An alliance is not a favor bank or a charm tour. It is a clear map of who can help, block, sway, fund, or wait. You study what each person wants protected, then ask in an order that makes the next talk safer.
breakdown.deepRead:
The mechanism is simple: people support plans that account for their risks. If your first pass is only a list of names, you miss the real map. A name list is not a power map. One stakeholder controls money, one controls a technical dependency, one holds trust with a group you barely know, and one can slow implementation without ever saying no.

Under Satya Nadella, Microsoft had to make a strategy believable beyond its own walls. Joining the Linux Foundation as a Platinum member in 2016 cost Microsoft an old posture before it could earn new trust. The visible cost mattered because Linux was not just an internal audience. It was an external community with its own memory, standards, and doubts. The move said Microsoft was willing to be judged by a group it could not command.

That is the pattern you can use in a smaller transition. Start with influence, not warmth. Mark who is already for the change, who may block it, who has not decided, who shapes opinion, and who holds resources. Then add the second column: what would make this worth their support? Support lasts when the plan pays others back. The order matters. A quiet yes from a trusted influencer may make a resource holder less nervous. A direct ask to a blocker may fail if no one else has made the path feel normal yet.
breakdown.fullRead:
A stakeholder map assumes you have something real to offer. When that precondition is missing, alliance work becomes pressure with better manners. People may still smile in the meeting, but they will not spend scarce time, reputation, or budget on a plan that only serves your first 90 days.

That is why the work is not broad networking. Broad networking can feel busy while the hard work waits. You leave several friendly calls with no clearer view of who can affect execution. Better diagnosis asks what each person can influence, what they fear losing, and what they need to see before they commit. If you do not know those answers, you are not building a coalition. You are collecting contacts.

IMD's First 90 Days structure makes this practical. The program protects time for diagnosis, planning, and coaching before urgent work eats the first weeks. That is not classroom polish. It makes the leader name the stakeholder environment while there is still room to learn. Once you have announced a plan, every later conversation sounds like a sale.

Satya Nadella's Microsoft also shows why rivals may still belong on the map. The company worked with Apple, Salesforce, IBM, and Dropbox while also competing with them. That does not mean every rival becomes a partner. It means the map follows strategic value, not old reflex. A former rival may hold adoption, legitimacy, or technical momentum that your title cannot reach.

Use the alliance map as a sorting tool, not a decoration. Put each important person or group into one of five plain buckets: supporters, blockers, undecideds, influencers, and resource holders. Then write one sentence beside each name: what they need from the transition. If the sentence is blank, schedule learning before asking. If the sentence is about your needs only, rewrite it from their side.

The cost often has to come first. You give up a cleaner launch story by asking a skeptic for conditions. You spend a scarce meeting slot with a quiet influencer instead of a senior fan. You let an external partner set part of the credibility test. For a while, that can feel like losing speed. In truth, it is how you stop paying a larger price later, when the deadline has passed and the chance to bring someone in early is gone.

The boundary is reciprocity. Coalition architecture quietly assumes there is shared value to find. When there is none, do not rename persuasion as alliance. Change the plan, change the ask, or admit that you are asking for compliance.

examples.title: Platinum Seat
examples.scenario: The badge cord scratches Amelia's neck as Amelia stands beside a partner desk covered with Microsoft speaker notes for the Linux Foundation announcement. The easy version would praise openness and keep control of the story. The harder version names the Platinum member step and accepts that an outside community will judge whether the shift is real.
examples.whatToDo: Amelia cuts the safest paragraph, keeps the public commitment, and writes the first follow-up around what the Linux community will need to see next.
examples.whyItMatters: The cost lands before the payoff. A visible alliance can make strategy believable only when the leader gives outsiders a real test of the change.

examples.title: New Altitude
examples.scenario: Brooklyn pinches the marker cap, then sets it beside a board headed Satya Nadella, Microsoft transition. Brooklyn asks Landon why someone who knows the company would map it again. Landon points to the blank partner lane and asks who can slow the work now. Brooklyn sees customers, engineers, and partners fill the lane. The old map is not wrong. It is too small.
examples.whatToDo: Brooklyn keeps the familiar names, then adds the groups that can shape enterprise movement from outside her old lane.
examples.whyItMatters: An internal promotion can make you overtrust old knowledge. The alliance map forces a fresh view before early decisions harden.

examples.title: Two Partner Lanes
examples.scenario: Two partner lanes. That is all Gemma has drawn under Satya Nadella and Microsoft before she catches her own error. Her first map treats cloud customers and engineers as enough because they are familiar. Nothing asks which outside partners can slow adoption, which internal groups hold trust, or who is undecided. The page looks tidy, but the alliance work is missing.
examples.whatToDo: Gemma stops mid-agenda, adds external partners and internal trust holders, and marks which conversation must happen before the first approval ask.
examples.whyItMatters: A familiar company can hide a changed role. The mistake shows up when the map leaves out people who now shape execution.

examples.title: Draft Before Send
examples.scenario: Jeanne is halfway through the transition lead's budget reply in the partner planning file when a 2016 Microsoft note about joining the Linux Foundation interrupts her. She does not send. The unsent draft becomes a memo instead: "Before approval, I need the credibility test. Public supporter: Linux Foundation. Risk: our old posture. Cost: let outsiders judge the shift."
examples.whatToDo: Jeanne turns the reply into a short sequence note and moves the budget ask behind one credibility conversation.
examples.whyItMatters: The pause protects the good version of the work. A fast ask can close the window before the right ally has made the change believable.

examples.title: Two Calendars
examples.scenario: The approval draft is due before the planning file closes, so Sophie writes Satya Nadella and Microsoft at the top before she touches the send button. She protects a block to ask which partners can make the cloud shift credible. Landon fills his open slots with friendly introductions. Sophie's calendar has sequence. Landon's has motion, but no map.
examples.whatToDo: Sophie uses the first block to sort partners before asking for commitments. Landon treats contact volume as progress and leaves sequencing for later.
examples.whyItMatters: Both calendars look active. Only one makes resistance visible before the plan is public and harder to change.

examples.title: Rival Logic
examples.scenario: Every partner conversation on the list asks Microsoft for help first. Landon keeps Apple, Salesforce, IBM, and Dropbox in a separate column marked rivals under Satya Nadella. His peer reads the column and says, "A rival is still a stakeholder if the work needs them." Landon does not erase the caution. He moves the names back onto the map.
examples.whatToDo: Landon keeps the competitive risk visible, then asks where shared strategic value makes a guarded alliance worth testing.
examples.whyItMatters: Alliance work is not friendship. It is a disciplined search for shared value across the boundaries that can make or break execution.

questions.prompt: A new leader lists everyone who attended the launch meeting and calls it a stakeholder map. Which correction fits the alliance move?
choices: Send one broad update so everyone hears the same plan at the same time.
Sort people by support, resistance, influence, and resources before sequencing talks.
Start with the friendliest names and let the map emerge from those calls.
questions.explanation: The alliance map separates supporters, blockers, undecideds, influencers, and resource holders. A raw contact list or friendly-first tour misses influence and sequence.

questions.prompt: A case note says Microsoft joined the Linux Foundation as a Platinum member in 2016 while outsiders watched the shift. What does that move show?
choices: External alliances can make a strategic change credible beyond the org chart.
Internal reporting lines can carry the shift once leaders explain the plan.
Public partnerships should wait until every internal concern has disappeared.
questions.explanation: The Linux Foundation move built credibility with an external ecosystem. The other answers keep alliance work inside the company or delay it until too late.

questions.prompt: A department head wants support for a plan and spends every meeting explaining why the plan matters to her first 90 days.
choices: Keep the pitch short so stakeholders do not feel overmanaged.
Ask for public backing from the most senior person in the room.
Show how the plan addresses the stakeholder's own risks and goals.
questions.explanation: Coalitions depend on reciprocal value. Support is stronger when stakeholders see their own needs in the plan, not only the leader's need for a win.

questions.prompt: A transition log shows the leader wrote the plan first and scheduled stakeholder calls only after announcing it.
choices: The order is efficient because stakeholders react better to a finished plan.
The order is harmless when the leader has enough prior experience.
The order is risky because resistance appears after commitments are public.
questions.explanation: Stakeholder diagnosis belongs inside transition work. Waiting until after the announcement invites resistance when the plan is already harder to change.

questions.prompt: A leader removes rival firms from the alliance map because working with competitors feels disloyal.
choices: Keep rivals off the map until the internal team has full agreement.
Test whether shared strategic value makes a guarded partnership useful.
Use rival names only as risks to mention in the communication plan.
questions.explanation: Nadella's Microsoft worked with companies it also competed with. The alliance logic follows strategic value, not old rivalry alone.

questions.prompt: A senior hire says a transition roadmap is unnecessary because she has led similar teams before.
choices: Accept the shortcut because experience replaces diagnosis in familiar roles.
Use the roadmap to link diagnosis with action before meetings become social calls.
Spend the roadmap time on morale events so people feel comfortable first.
questions.explanation: The IMD roadmap links diagnosis to action planning. Experience helps, but it does not reveal this role's hidden constraints without inquiry.

questions.prompt: A calendar review shows a new leader postponed alliance work until the formal review cycle.
choices: That is fine because the first 90 days are only an HR label.
That is fine if the leader keeps a careful contact list meanwhile.
That is risky because early actions shape trust before formal reviews.
questions.explanation: The first 90 days matter because stakeholders form working assumptions early. Waiting for formal review gives away room to maneuver.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder spreadsheet has columns for title, email, and meeting date. The plan still keeps stalling.
choices: Add influence, interest, support level, and resource control to guide the sequence.
Add more meeting dates so the leader can increase contact volume quickly.
Add seniority rank so the leader can ask the hierarchy in order.
questions.explanation: A useful alliance map captures influence, interests, and sequence. More contact or hierarchy alone does not show who can help or block execution.

questions.prompt: A platform team wants a developer community to believe its new direction, but the team can only control internal messages.
choices: Make a visible external commitment that lets the community judge the shift.
Keep the message internal until the community asks for proof of change.
Focus on executive sponsorship because outsiders cannot affect implementation.
questions.explanation: The Microsoft and Linux Foundation case shows external partners can control legitimacy and momentum. Internal messages alone may not make the shift credible.

reviewCards.front: What does coalition architecture ask you to map before asking for support?
reviewCards.back: Name who can change execution, what they care about, what they need from you, and which early yes could make the next talk easier.

reviewCards.front: Which five groups belong on the alliance map?
reviewCards.back: Use the source's five groups: supporters, blockers, undecideds, influencers, and resource holders. Each group needs a different next move.

reviewCards.front: Why is likability too weak to carry alliance work?
reviewCards.back: Charm fades when the plan does not answer the other person's risks or goals. Durable support comes from reciprocal value.

reviewCards.front: How would accelerated learning agenda (Ch 2) change your alliance work here?
reviewCards.back: It would make you learn before asking. Use repeatable questions to test what stakeholders value, fear, and control, then build the alliance sequence from that evidence.

reviewCards.front: What does Microsoft's Linux Foundation move teach about external alliances?
reviewCards.back: Some allies sit outside the reporting line. A visible external commitment can make a new strategy believable where authority alone cannot reach.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning a contact list into an alliance map. For each important person or group, name their map slot, what they need, and what you can offer before you ask for support.

ifThenPlans.context: Your stakeholder list is only names and titles
ifThenPlans.plan: If the list has no influence or resource notes, then add the map slot before scheduling the next conversation.

ifThenPlans.context: A planned ask mostly explains what you need
ifThenPlans.plan: If the ask starts with your win, then rewrite it around the stakeholder's risk, goal, or constraint.

ifThenPlans.context: You are about to announce before diagnosing support
ifThenPlans.plan: If the plan is nearly public, then move one stakeholder learning conversation ahead of the announcement.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before one real reply in the next day, put your calendar beside the draft, move one alliance conversation earlier, and rehearse the ask once.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one workweek, keep a daily alliance log with these columns: stakeholder, map slot, their risk, value offered, next sequence move.

memorableLines.text: Authority opens doors; alliances move work.
A name list is not a power map.
Support lasts when the plan pays others back.

chapters.title: Manage Yourself
chapters.hook: A 90-day calendar can fail because one coaching hour disappears.
chapters.counterintuition: Pressure can make nonstop availability look responsible. In fact, it can starve the reflection and support that keep judgment clean.
chapters.tryThisNow: When one more transition meeting starts to feel harmless, block 15 minutes and record the boundary you will use to protect diagnosis time.
chapters.keyTakeaway: In a transition, energy, support, boundaries, reflection, and judgment are work tools: protect them before pressure turns old habits into bad decisions.

breakdown.fastRead:
The phone keeps lighting up while the reply you meant to send sinks under a wall of new pings. By night, the missed note has cooled a relationship you needed. That is how a transition starts to manage you.

The danger is not only being tired. It is what fatigue does to judgment. You skip the hard read, take the familiar task, and call it urgency. Stamina protects judgment.

Manage yourself means guarding the fuel, challenge, limits, thinking space, and clear choices that pressure tries to steal. When those stay intact, you can keep learning while people watch your first moves.
breakdown.deepRead:
Pressure narrows the room inside your head. A new role floods you with meetings, private worries, and people testing how you decide. If there is no space to think, you start treating the loudest item as the most important one.

That is why transition stamina is a business tool, not a wellness prize. Energy lets you notice weak signals. Support lets someone challenge your first story before it hardens. Boundaries stop the day from being filled by other people's anxiety. Reflection turns raw meetings into judgment.

The IMD First 90 Days program makes this concrete by putting diagnosis, action planning, and coaching into a fixed structure. The detail that matters is not school polish. It is that transition work gets time on the calendar before crisis fills every open space. A leader who protects reflection is not hiding from the job. Meetings create data; reflection makes it useful.

Old strengths can become hiding places. A leader who won praise for fast fixes may rush to fix before listening. The familiar move feels calm because it worked before. In the new role, it may be exactly what blocks learning.

The practical move is to pause at the first pull toward speed. Ask what is being protected: attention, image, comfort, or real value. Then choose the next boundary, support check, or thinking block. The strongest leaders do not spend all day available. They stay available for the right work.
breakdown.fullRead:
Quentin is ten minutes from a team call when the group chat starts to flood. One thread needs a budget answer, one carries a rumor, and one has the buried message that matters: a cautious warning from the person closest to the customer handoff. If Quentin answers in order of noise, the signal dies in the scroll.

This is the first hard edge of self-management. The outer work looks like stakeholder management. The inner work is choosing which signal gets your mind while your status is still forming. In the first 90 days, people learn your pattern fast. Do you reward noise? Do you punish bad news? Do you disappear into private strain? The answers shape what people bring you next.

A disciplined review cadence helps because it makes reality easier to face as a group. A regular rhythm keeps problems from becoming private hero work. The lesson for self-management is not to copy a meeting format by rote. It is to use routine as protection. When the right facts have a place to go, the leader does not have to chase every fire alone.

The self-management system has five parts: energy, support, boundaries, reflection, and judgment. Energy is not just sleep; it is the attention you have left for hard facts. Support is not venting; it is trusted challenge from someone who can ask, "What else could be true?" Boundaries are not walls; they are choices about which work deserves access to your best hours. Reflection is not daydreaming; it is the step that turns meetings into sense. Judgment is what the other four are protecting.

The strongest sign that you need the system is a familiar pull. You want to do the work that made you successful before. You want to answer fast, solve fast, and prove that the new role was safe in your hands. That can be useful when a true crisis needs action. It can also be fear wearing a useful jacket. Familiar work can soothe you while it blinds you.

A support network is the antidote to private certainty. Coaching in the IMD transition structure matters because a leader can become trapped inside a first impression. A trusted outsider, peer, or coach does not take the decision away. They slow down the story long enough for better questions to enter.

This idea breaks in a live emergency where delay would harm people or destroy trust. If payroll is broken, a safety issue is active, or a legal deadline closes today, reflection time cannot become a shield against action. Move, then review. The boundary is simple: protect thinking when the cost of delay is learning; act fast when the cost of delay is harm.

Most transition damage is quieter. It comes from weeks of tiny leaks: the skipped walk, the support call never made, the boundary sentence swallowed, the late reply that cools an ally. You do not manage yourself to feel calm. You manage yourself so pressure does not get to make your decisions.

examples.title: Adam's Review Rhythm
examples.scenario: "Bring the real numbers, not the brave ones," Adam says at the conference room table. His first week looked different: after studying the Ford 2006 operating cadence, he still accepted every operating problem alone and left with a legal pad full of private fixes. By the next review, the same leaders bring facts into one shared rhythm. Adam is no longer the only place reality can land.
examples.whatToDo: Adam keeps the shared review on the calendar and asks each lead for facts, risks, and next commitments instead of taking every loose issue into private rescue work.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows why cadence protects stamina. A leader can create transparency without becoming the only engine that keeps the transition moving.

examples.title: Sierra Catches Speed
examples.scenario: The clean learning plan sits beside Sierra's crowded phone, and both are hers. In the coffee shop line before a stakeholder visit, she starts typing an answer to a problem she has not diagnosed. The IMD First 90 Days method was supposed to make entry a roadmap, not a reflex. The barista calls her name, and Sierra hears how automatic the draft sounds. She deletes the promise and writes the question she still needs answered.
examples.whatToDo: Sierra turns the stakeholder visit into a listening pass. She asks what constraint, risk, and evidence should shape any promise.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery begins when she notices her own pull toward speed. Self-management is the pause that keeps experience from hardening into a bad shortcut.

examples.title: Kelsey's Coaching Slot
examples.scenario: The transition calendar lands with Kelsey after the dashboard shows two owners for the same customer metric. The family group chat keeps asking when she will be home, while the open slot for IMD's 3 half days plus individual coaching sits between two briefings. She wants the neat answer now. She also knows this is the one conversation likely to keep her first story from becoming too certain.
examples.whatToDo: Kelsey keeps the coaching block intact and moves a lower-value briefing instead of surrendering the one conversation built to challenge her assumptions.
examples.whyItMatters: The thought process exposes the real pressure. Support can feel optional until isolation starts turning early impressions into fixed beliefs.

examples.title: Piper Allocates Attention
examples.scenario: The calendar invite slides from tentative to accepted before Piper touches the keyboard. At the kitchen table, the first-month grid is almost full: stakeholder calls, team reviews, travel, and one empty block. The IMD First 90 Days roadmap gives her the scarce choice before action starts: attention. If she gives the last clear block away, the meetings will have no place to become judgment.
examples.whatToDo: Piper protects the empty block for reflection and moves a lower-value update to email before the month can fill itself for her.
examples.whyItMatters: Planning is part of self-management. Meetings produce signals, but a leader needs protected time to turn those signals into choices.

examples.title: Bennett's Stuck Key
examples.scenario: The hotel key sticks halfway in the door, and Bennett's boss-call brief still will not load. The IMD First 90 Days structure includes coaching, making him wonder what his one quiet hour is for before the call. Bennett is torn between calling a trusted peer and admitting his read may be thin, or going in alone with a story that may sound firm before it has been tested.
examples.whatToDo: Bennett calls the peer and asks for pressure on his assumptions, not sympathy. He enters the boss call with a cleaner story and one unresolved question.
examples.whyItMatters: Support is not weakness when it improves judgment before a decision goes public. The cost of looking certain too soon is often higher.

examples.title: Quentin Yields the Hour
examples.scenario: The phone buzzes against the wood of Quentin's apartment desk during a Friday peer call, and the buzz is his whole argument. "Every stakeholder wants an hour," he says. Adam answers, "IMD treats First 90 Days work as diagnosis, planning, and coaching. Do not turn that roadmap into a waiting room." Quentin says, "Skipping them looks careless." Adam says, "Skipping reflection makes the meetings careless." Quentin exhales. "I will protect the hour."
examples.whatToDo: Quentin yields to the stronger read and writes the boundary note before adding more meetings. The protected hour stays tied to diagnosis, not comfort.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange shows a boundary under social pressure. Availability can look generous while it quietly steals the judgment the transition needs.

questions.prompt: A new leader answers late messages until midnight and starts treating the loudest request as the safest one. Which reading best fits the risk?
choices: The late messages mainly show that the leader needs a tighter inbox rule.
The late messages prove stakeholder access is the main source of trust.
The late messages are draining energy in a way that can distort judgment.
questions.explanation: Energy management matters because fatigue changes what the leader notices and decides. An inbox rule may help, but the deeper risk is judgment under pressure.

questions.prompt: A team log shows full stakeholder days but no protected thinking blocks during the entry period. What should be added first?
choices: More stakeholder meetings so the leader can gather a wider set of raw comments.
A reflection block that turns the meeting data into patterns and choices.
A shorter status update so the leader can fit another briefing into the week.
questions.explanation: Meetings create data, but reflection turns it into judgment. More meetings can feel useful while crowding out the work that makes the data matter.

questions.prompt: When a senior hire treats the first month as a string of casual introductions, which correction fits the First 90 Days approach?
choices: Use a roadmap that links diagnosis, stakeholder learning, and action planning.
Rely on experience to decide which meetings matter after they happen.
Keep the month flexible so no early plan narrows the leader's options.
questions.explanation: The roadmap keeps entry from becoming loose social motion. Experience helps, but it does not reveal hidden constraints without planned inquiry.

questions.prompt: A leader keeps using the fast-fix style that made her successful in her old role. Why is that habit especially tempting now?
choices: It proves the old role and the new role share the same hidden constraints.
It reduces uncertainty because familiar work feels safer under pressure.
It shows technical skill is the only reason old habits fail in new roles.
questions.explanation: The trap is emotional as well as technical. Familiar work can calm the leader while blocking the diagnosis the new role needs.

questions.prompt: A new director has a strong first story about why the team is missing targets. What should a support network do before the story hardens?
choices: Protect the story from challenge until the director sounds more confident.
Test the story with trusted challenge while the evidence is still fresh.
Replace the director's judgment with the network's safer group view.
questions.explanation: Support helps by challenging early narratives before they become fixed. It should sharpen the leader's judgment, not shield or replace it.

questions.prompt: When a new country lead sees her individual coaching slot marked optional after a rough first week, which reason best protects it?
choices: It lets senior leaders process pressure alone with a more polished schedule.
It turns the transition into general career advice with fewer hard questions.
It keeps the leader's private interpretation open to challenge before isolation sets in.
questions.explanation: Coaching challenges private interpretations before they harden. The near misses either keep the leader isolated or soften the transition into generic advice.

questions.prompt: A colleague calls the first 90 days an HR phrase and plans to wait for the formal review. Which reply fits the transition risk?
choices: Early actions shape trust and expectations before formal reviews arrive.
Formal reviews are the only moments when stakeholders update their views.
The calendar period matters mainly because onboarding forms are due.
questions.explanation: Stakeholders form working assumptions early. Treating the period as paperwork misses how quickly trust and room to move get shaped.

questions.prompt: Your first week in a visible role is filled with travel, late calls, and rushed decisions. Which self-management move best protects performance?
choices: Treat the strain as private and push through until the role feels stable.
Add more meetings so stakeholders can see commitment through availability.
Manage energy as part of the work because tired judgment changes decisions.
questions.explanation: Energy is tied to judgment, not separate from performance. Pushing through may look committed while making urgent signals seem more important than they are.

questions.prompt: A calendar review shows every open block getting traded for another stakeholder call. Which boundary best protects judgment?
choices: Keep one protected block so the calls can be turned into judgment.
Accept every call now and look for thinking time after the transition settles.
Cut stakeholder calls broadly so the calendar feels less exposed.
questions.explanation: Protected reflection helps convert raw data into judgment. Accepting every call repeats the trap, while broad cutting can dodge needed learning.

reviewCards.front: What is transition stamina protecting?
reviewCards.back: It protects judgment during the first 90 days. Energy, support, boundaries, and reflection keep pressure from turning urgency and old habits into poor decisions.

reviewCards.front: Why is managing energy a leadership issue, not just a private wellness issue?
reviewCards.back: Fatigue changes what a leader notices, avoids, and decides. In a visible transition, tired judgment can become a business risk before anyone names it.

reviewCards.front: How does a support network improve early transition judgment?
reviewCards.back: It tests first stories before they become fixed. A trusted peer or coach can ask what else might be true while the evidence is still fresh.

reviewCards.front: Why can old success habits become dangerous in a new role?
reviewCards.back: They feel safe under pressure, so the leader may repeat them before learning the new role's constraints. Familiar work can soothe anxiety while blocking diagnosis.

reviewCards.front: What are the five parts of the self-management system?
reviewCards.back: The five parts are energy, support, boundaries, reflection, and judgment. The first four protect the last one during the transition window.

reviewCards.front: Where does team architecture (Ch 7) help here, and where would leaning on it mislead you?
reviewCards.back: Team architecture helps you see role fit, norms, and cadence. It misleads if you blame the team before checking whether your fatigue, isolation, or old habits are distorting the read.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice guarding the time and support that keep pressure from choosing for you. Protect the Judgment Block means you notice when availability is crowding out diagnosis, then put one boundary, support check, or reflection block where it belongs. The point is not comfort; the point is better decisions.

ifThenPlans.context: The day fills with meetings and no thinking space remains
ifThenPlans.plan: If the calendar has no room to turn meetings into judgment, then Protect the Judgment Block by moving one update to writing and holding one reflection block.

ifThenPlans.context: A familiar old-role fix starts to feel soothing
ifThenPlans.plan: If the old move feels safe before the new facts are clear, then Protect the Judgment Block by writing the unanswered question before acting.

ifThenPlans.context: An early story about a person or team starts to feel certain
ifThenPlans.plan: If the story feels finished too soon, then Protect the Judgment Block by asking one trusted peer to challenge the read.

ifThenPlans.context: Late work starts making loud requests feel important
ifThenPlans.plan: If fatigue makes the loudest item feel safest, then Protect the Judgment Block by deferring one nonurgent reply until after rest and review.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, when pressure makes another request feel easy to accept, put a 15-minute judgment block on the calendar and write the boundary note you will send.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, rehearse the boundary under real conditions: decline or defer one lower-value request, keep the protected block, and note what judgment it improved.

memorableLines.text: Stamina protects judgment.
Meetings create data; reflection makes it useful.
Familiar work can soothe you while it blinds you.

chapters.title: Accelerate Everyone
chapters.hook: A calendar invite leaves HR as a welcome note and returns with sponsors, coaching, and diagnosis attached.
chapters.counterintuition: Why do experienced companies still let new leaders sink or swim? They standardize welcome tasks before they standardize language, sponsors, coaching, and diagnosis.
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next handoff between tasks, spend ten minutes writing one line for the next person: "This transition needs ___ before action."
