chapters.keyTakeaway: Make transition work a shared system: give leaders common language, sponsors, coaching, and adaptive diagnosis, then keep each role from becoming the same checklist.

breakdown.fastRead:
Colby drags a welcome checklist into the shared folder and feels useful for about ten seconds. Then the old belief shows up: a strong leader should figure out the role alone. The checklist sends forms, badges, and links, but it does not tell anyone who should open doors, what situation the leader is entering, or where coaching begins. Shared language speeds the room.

The final move in The First 90 Days is not a private trick for one ambitious manager. It is an organizational habit. HR, talent teams, sponsors, and executives can give each new leader the same basic words for diagnosis and planning. Then they must adapt the support to the role. A checklist cannot diagnose a role.
breakdown.deepRead:
Transition support works because it moves the first handoff upstream. Before the leader is tired, buried in meetings, and guessing who matters, the organization can name the work: diagnose the situation, map stakeholders, agree on expectations, build the team, and plan early wins. The first handoff teaches the system.

IMD presents First 90 Days work as a roadmap for a new role. Its structure joins scheduled program time with individual coaching, which matters because a roadmap without coaching can become homework. Coaching gives the leader a place to test the plan while the pressure is still real. Peer learning adds another mirror. When leaders compare transition patterns, one person's hidden trap becomes another person's early warning.

The scale of the method explains why this can work beyond one desk. IMD reports more than 1.5 million copies sold and 23 different languages. Those numbers do not make the idea true by themselves. They show that many organizations already recognize the same pain: new leaders arrive fast, politics form early, and private improvisation wastes time.

The danger is flattening the method into one script. A startup role is not a turnaround. A realignment is not a sustaining-success assignment. The shared part is the language and the support. The adaptive part is the diagnosis. Support scales only when judgment stays awake.
breakdown.fullRead:
The cost of accelerating everyone is that the organization gives up the easy story of heroic entry. It can no longer shrug when a new leader misses a sponsor, misreads the role, or spends the first month with ten half-finished threads and nothing finished. Someone has to prepare the handoff before the person arrives.

That cost shows up in small rooms. Colby cannot just send the welcome packet and close the ticket. She has to ask who the sponsor is, what situation the leader is entering, and where the first coaching touch belongs. Deborah cannot count a full calendar as support if every meeting is a social call. Connor cannot tell a new leader to move fast and then hide the real power map.

The myth says better leaders need less structure. The practice says better leaders use structure faster. A clear roadmap does not make the person weak. It stops the first weeks from becoming a scavenger hunt.

The IMD structure is a useful signal because it turns transition work into time, coaching, and repeatable language. Three half days do not solve entry by themselves. Individual coaching does not solve it either. The value is that the organization stops pretending a major role change can be handled by a welcome email and a crowded calendar. A calendar can be full and still leave the leader alone.

Still, the support must stay honest. If every new leader gets the same first-month script, the method has been made cheaper and dumber. A leader entering a turnaround needs different questions from a leader protecting a strong business. A leader in realignment needs to find the hidden gap between current habits and needed change. A leader in sustaining success needs to protect what works before improving it.

Here is where boss alignment negotiation from chapter 5 fits. The boss conversation makes success conditions explicit for one relationship. The organization has to build the same clarity into the handoff system. The leader still has to negotiate expectations, style, resources, and development needs. The system makes sure those talks are not left to luck.

The tradeoff is attention. HR, talent, sponsors, and executives must spend a little attention before the transition becomes urgent. They must write the first handoff better, open doors sooner, and stay close enough to coach without taking the role away. That is less tidy than sending a packet. It is also fairer than watching another leader learn the hidden rules after the room has already judged them.

examples.title: Mathieu's Thread Pin
examples.scenario: Dragging the IMD First 90 Days program invite into the HR text thread, Mathieu pauses. Mathieu: Sponsor map before welcome email. Colby: We already send the packet. Deborah: Leaders keep asking who owns individual coaching. Mathieu: Then packet is late. The thread gains three owners: sponsor intro, STARS question, coaching slot. One small note changes the handoff.
examples.whatToDo: Mathieu pins the missing handoff line and asks who owns it. He keeps the text thread on sponsor access, diagnosis, and coaching instead of letting the packet count as support.
examples.whyItMatters: The small act cascades because it changes who acts next. A shared framework starts to work when one handoff names the support the new leader would otherwise have to hunt down.

examples.title: Colby's Restart
examples.scenario: Colby is filling the usual welcome checklist when the returned phone call buzzes beside her keyboard. The sponsor asks whether IMD's First 90 Days work needs coaching or just slides. Colby stops with her cursor on "send packet." She deletes that line, writes "roadmap plus individual coaching," and restarts the call with the role diagnosis first.
examples.whatToDo: Colby pauses the routine and rewrites the handoff before she sends anything. She makes the program a coached roadmap, not a folder of slides.
examples.whyItMatters: The reset changes the handoff before it reaches the leader. If the first handoff stays generic, the leader inherits mental clutter before the role even begins.

examples.title: Deborah's Badge Line
examples.scenario: The enrollment window is closing while Deborah smooths a curled badge on the edge of her office desk. The IMD note says The First 90 Days has reached more than 1.5 million copies and 23 different languages. Her pen hovers over one blank line for this leader: "first diagnosis question." The big reach shrinks to the next sentence she must hand over.
examples.whatToDo: Deborah turns the adoption fact into one local handoff line. She writes the diagnosis question on the badge packet before the leader arrives.
examples.whyItMatters: Scale only helps if it reaches the next person. The numbers explain why the language travels, but the handoff makes it usable.

examples.title: Connor's Same Script
examples.scenario: The late-afternoon sponsor call has one page for every role, and none of the roles are the same. Connor says, "So everyone gets the same First 90 Days week?" Stella answers, "IMD gives us shared words, not same moves." Connor taps the plan beside his phone. "Startup, turnaround, realignment, sustaining success?" Stella says, "Different diagnosis. Shared language. That is the line."
examples.whatToDo: Connor keeps the shared language but refuses the same action plan for every role. He asks Stella to attach a diagnosis step before the first-week schedule.
examples.whyItMatters: Scaling the method does not mean copying one calendar. The organization can standardize support while still asking what kind of situation the leader is entering.

examples.title: Stella Hears the Gap
examples.scenario: "She still doesn't know who can unblock finance," someone says near Stella's desk, and Stella stops typing the intake summary. Her IMD First 90 Days form promises individual coaching, yet her own line says, "leader owns stakeholder outreach." She sees the error before she finishes it. HR, L&D, and Talent Management are supposed to equip the transition.
examples.whatToDo: Stella changes the intake summary while it is still open. She adds sponsor access, stakeholder support, and a coaching check before the leader has to ask again.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery matters because the error sounds responsible. Making only the leader accountable can hide the support the organization controls.

examples.title: Coralie's Decision Memo
examples.scenario: "Keep it simple," Coralie says, then writes the memo instead of adding another meeting. Decision: use First 90 Days language for every leadership entry. Requirements: sponsor map, situation diagnosis, team questions, coaching path. Guardrail: no copied checklist. IMD's long transition work proves the tools can repeat; the role diagnosis still has to be fresh.
examples.whatToDo: Coralie turns the decision memo into a handoff rule. The artifact names the repeatable tools and adds a guardrail against using one checklist for every transition.
examples.whyItMatters: The memo makes the system visible. It gives future leaders a standard starting point while preserving the judgment their roles still require.

questions.prompt: A sponsor says a new leader can wait until the first formal review to learn how people see her. Which response fits the 90-day window?
choices: The first weeks can stay informal because the review will reset expectations.
The first weeks matter because people form working assumptions early.
The first weeks mainly test whether the leader can ignore first impressions.
questions.explanation: The 90-day window matters because trust and expectations form early. Waiting for a formal review lets assumptions harden first.

questions.prompt: A new executive has years of experience, so the company plans only welcome meetings. What is missing from the roadmap idea?
choices: Experience still needs diagnosis and action planning for the new role.
Experience replaces the need for structured inquiry in most transitions.
Experience matters most when meetings stay open and unplanned.
questions.explanation: The roadmap links diagnosis to action. Experience helps, but it does not reveal the new role's hidden limits by itself.

questions.prompt: A talent team sees that First 90 Days language is already common across many firms and languages. What should it infer?
choices: The reach makes the method useful mainly as a private reading plan.
The reach proves every role should use the same entry checklist.
The reach can support a shared transition language across leaders.
questions.explanation: Broad adoption supports common language. It does not turn the method into private self-help or one fixed checklist.

questions.prompt: A leader says transition success is only her job because she accepted the role. Which reply matches the source?
choices: The leader owns all preparation because sponsors should avoid shaping entry.
The organization also shapes preparation, coaching, expectations, and access.
The organization should wait until the leader asks before offering support.
questions.explanation: IMD speaks to HR, L&D, and talent professionals because organizations shape the support around role entry.

questions.prompt: A log shows the same first-month checklist used for a startup, a realignment, and a sustaining-success role. What is the problem?
choices: Shared support has replaced diagnosis with one script for different roles.
Shared support has failed because leaders used the same vocabulary.
Shared support has gone too slowly because coaching was included.
questions.explanation: The scalable part is language and support. The action plan still has to adapt to the situation diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A peer group compares transition patterns after each leader's first sponsor meetings. What does that add?
choices: It replaces coaching because peers can make the plan final.
It proves reading the framework once is enough for use under pressure.
It helps leaders spot common traps before facing them alone.
questions.explanation: Peer learning helps under pressure because leaders see patterns and traps across transitions, not just in their own role.

questions.prompt: An executive argues that every transition is too unique for a common method. Which answer preserves the hard edge?
choices: A common method should remove role differences so leaders can move faster.
A common method should stay private because role differences defeat shared tools.
A common method can share tools while diagnosis protects role differences.
questions.explanation: Repeated use can create reusable tools. Diagnosis keeps those tools from flattening the role's real situation.

questions.prompt: A program dashboard shows leaders getting the same sponsor script across different STARS situations. What should the reader flag?
choices: The sponsor script is useful because shared wording removes the need for diagnosis.
The sponsor script is risky because shared wording is being used as identical action.
The sponsor script is irrelevant because STARS situations cannot share any language.
questions.explanation: Shared words help people coordinate, but identical action choices ignore the different situations the diagnosis is meant to reveal.

questions.prompt: A talent partner wants one practical sign that transition acceleration is becoming an organizational capability. Which sign fits?
choices: Sponsors provide resources before and during entry, not only after trouble appears.
Sponsors let new leaders prove themselves before opening stakeholder access.
Sponsors keep coaching separate from onboarding so leaders stay independent.
questions.explanation: The organization accelerates transitions when it shapes preparation, coaching, expectations, and access before the leader is left alone.

reviewCards.front: What does it mean to make transition acceleration an organizational capability?
reviewCards.back: It means HR, talent, sponsors, and executives share language, coaching, roadmaps, and stakeholder support so each new leader does not invent the entry process alone.

reviewCards.front: Why is one shared checklist a weak version of transition acceleration?
reviewCards.back: A checklist can carry useful steps, but it cannot diagnose the role. The scalable part is the common language and support; the action plan must still fit the situation.

reviewCards.front: How do coaching and peer learning change the roadmap?
reviewCards.back: They keep the roadmap from becoming paperwork. Coaching gives the leader feedback under pressure, and peers help reveal traps before each person meets them alone.

reviewCards.front: Why does broad First 90 Days adoption matter to an organization?
reviewCards.back: The reported reach shows that the language already travels across many settings. That makes it easier for a company to use the method as a shared transition vocabulary.

reviewCards.front: How does boss alignment negotiation (Ch 5) connect to Accelerate Everyone's core move in one sentence?
reviewCards.back: Boss alignment negotiation makes one relationship explicit; Accelerate Everyone asks the organization to build that clarity into every transition handoff before assumptions harden.

reviewCards.front: What price does an organization pay to accelerate everyone?
reviewCards.back: It gives up the lazy comfort of sink-or-swim entry. Sponsors and talent teams must spend attention earlier, write better handoffs, and stay close enough to coach.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice writing one handoff line before a transition task leaves your hands. The line names what the next person needs before action: sponsor access, diagnosis, coaching, or a clear owner. This keeps support practical without turning every role into the same script.

ifThenPlans.context: A new leader receives a welcome packet
ifThenPlans.plan: If the packet is ready but support is unnamed, then write the handoff line that names the sponsor, access point, or coaching owner.

ifThenPlans.context: A template is about to be reused
ifThenPlans.plan: If the template fits too neatly, then write the handoff line that names the role's situation before copying the schedule.

ifThenPlans.context: A meeting risks becoming a social call
ifThenPlans.plan: If the agenda has no diagnosis, then write the handoff line that turns the meeting into one question and one next action.

ifThenPlans.context: A leader is applying the framework alone
ifThenPlans.plan: If the plan is private and pressure is rising, then write the handoff line that asks which peer or coach can test the next move.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Over the next day, write one handoff line at each transition between tasks: "Before action, this needs ___." Use it only when real work passes to another person or your future self.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Ask one person this week to flag when you treat a transition as sink-or-swim. Compare notes once and rewrite one handoff line from what they noticed.

memorableLines.text: Shared language speeds the room.
A checklist cannot diagnose a role.
Support scales only when judgment stays awake.
